I. Theory: Lý thuyết nền tảng & Bẫy kinh điển
1. Bản chất & Format Part 1
• Hình thức: Cuộc hội thoại đối thoại (Dialogue) giữa hai người trong ngữ cảnh đời sống thường nhật (Social / Transactional context).
• Vai trò nhân vật: Một người là người cung cấp thông tin/nhân viên tiếp nhận (lễ tân khách sạn, thư ký trung tâm, tư vấn viên) và người còn lại là khách hàng/ứng viên.
• Số lượng câu hỏi: 10 câu (Questions 1 – 10).
• Dạng bài thống trị: Điền từ vào chỗ trống: Điền mẫu đơn (Form completion), Ghi chú tóm tắt (Notes completion), Điền bảng (Table completion).
• Mục tiêu khảo thí: Khả năng nghe và trích xuất các dữ liệu sự thật cụ thể: Tên họ người, địa chỉ, số điện thoại, ngày tháng, thời gian, số tiền, loại dịch vụ, phương tiện di chuyển.
2. Ma trận Quy tắc đếm từ & 5 Cơ chế Bẫy thông tin Part 1

theory.text: 3. Bốn bẫy ngữ âm & chính tả kinh điển
Bẫy 1: Nhầm lẫn bảng chữ cái tiếng Anh
Các ký tự dễ nhầm lẫn nhất khi người bản xứ đánh vần nhanh:
• Nguyên âm: A (/eɪ/) – E (/iː/) – I (/aɪ/). Thí sinh thường viết E khi nghe thấy âm /iː/, nhưng lại viết nhầm A thành E.
• Cặp phụ âm: G (/dʒiː/) vs J (/dʒeɪ/); B (/biː/) vs P (/piː/); C (/siː/) vs S (/es/).
• Ký tự đặc biệt: H (/eɪtʃ/ - rất dễ nhầm với số 8 /eɪt/), W (/ˈdʌbəl.juː/), Y (/waɪ/), Z (Anh-Anh đọc là zed /zed/, Anh-Mỹ đọc là zee /ziː/).
Bẫy 2: Phân biệt số đuôi "-teen" vs "-ty"
• Đuôi -teen (13–19): Trọng âm rơi mạnh vào âm tiết thứ hai: four-TEEN (/fɔːˈtiːn/), fif-TEEN (/fɪfˈtiːn/), nguyên âm kéo dài.
• Đuôi -ty (30–90): Trọng âm rơi mạnh vào âm tiết đầu tiên: FOR-ty (/ˈfɔːti/), FIF-ty (/ˈfɪfti/), âm cuối dứt khoát và ngắn.
Bẫy 3: Số điện thoại, mã bưu điện (Postcodes) & địa chỉ
• Số 0 trong số điện thoại thường được đọc là "oh" (/oʊ/), đôi khi đọc là "zero".
• Hai số giống nhau đọc là "double" (ví dụ 77 = double seven), ba số giống nhau đọc là "triple" (ví dụ 888 = triple eight).
• Mã bưu điện tại Anh (UK Postcode) xen kẽ chữ và số: ví dụ SW1A 2AA, EC4V 5BY.
Bẫy 4: Danh từ số ít vs số nhiều (Singular vs Plural)

Nghe sót âm đuôi /s/ hoặc /z/ là lỗi mất điểm phổ biến nhất trong Part 1. Nếu băng đọc "We have four brand-new indoor courts" mà bạn viết court (số ít), câu đó bị tính là sai ngữ pháp và không có điểm.

guide.text: II. Guide cách làm bài: Quy trình 4 giai đoạn chuẩn quốc tế
Giai đoạn 1: Pre-listening (Tận dụng 30–45 giây trước khi nghe)
1. Đọc kỹ giới hạn từ: Khoanh tròn cụm từ quy định số từ (ví dụ NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER).
2. Đọc tiêu đề biểu mẫu: Xác định xem ai đang nói chuyện với ai về chủ đề gì (thuê xe, mua bảo hiểm, đăng ký lớp học...).
3. Phân tích từng chỗ trống:
• Xác định từ loại: Chỗ trống cần điền Danh từ (Noun), Tính từ (Adjective), Động từ (Verb), hay Con số (Number)?
• Xác định trường nghĩa: Cần điền tên riêng, số điện thoại, ngày tháng, tên căn bệnh, phương tiện hay dụng cụ?
• Kiểm tra từ in sẵn: Có sẵn ký hiệu £, $, pm, hay các từ bổ nghĩa phía trước/sau không?
Giai đoạn 2: While-listening (Trong khi nghe)
1. Dùng tai nghe và mắt dẫn đường: Mắt luôn nhìn trước chỗ trống 1 câu để đón đầu thông tin.
2. Bắt từ mỏ neo (Anchor words): Chờ đợi các từ không thể thay đổi (tên riêng, tiêu đề mục con) để biết băng đã nói tới câu nào.
3. Giữ bút chờ lời xác nhận cuối cùng: Không vội vàng viết ngay đáp án đầu tiên nghe thấy, đề phòng bẫy tự sửa lỗi (self-correction).
Giai đoạn 3: Post-listening (Rà soát nhanh 30 giây)
1. Kiểm tra chính tả: Đã viết hoa chữ cái đầu cho danh từ riêng chưa (London, Wednesday, Fairview Avenue)?
2. Kiểm tra số ít/số nhiều: Câu có mạo từ a/an không? Nếu không có mạo từ trước một danh từ đếm được, khả năng rất cao từ đó phải có đuôi -s/-es.
3. Kiểm tra giới hạn từ: Đã vô tình viết thừa giới từ hoặc đơn vị tiền tệ có sẵn chưa?
Giai đoạn 4: Post-test Audit (Lập nhật ký lỗi sau khi làm đề)
Ghi chép lại lỗi sai vào bảng Error Log: Sai do nghe nhầm âm, sai do chính tả, hay sai do mắc bẫy đổi ý định?

rows: Trích dẫn Audio Script & Giải thích bẫy
Đánh vần từng chữ cái: B-R-A-I-T-H-W-A-I-T-E. Bắt buộc viết hoa.
"I was born on the 18th of August, 1994." Số ngày và năm đã in sẵn trên đề.
Số nhà riêng bị loại vì ban ngày khách không ở nhà. Số di động là số chuẩn.
Đánh vần: F-A-I-R-V-I-E-W. Từ Avenue đã in sẵn trên đề.
Mã bưu điện UK: 3 ký tự đầu cách 3 ký tự sau.
Gói Gold bị khách từ chối vì quá đắt so với ngân sách ("excessive for my budget"). Khách chọn gói Silver.
Bơi lội chỉ là sở thích phụ, môn thể thao chính trong nhà khách muốn chơi là tennis.
Danh từ số ít: chấn thương bả vai do chơi bóng bầu dục trước đây ("weak left shoulder").
Khách từ chối trả trọn gói 1 năm mà muốn trả theo từng tháng ("on a monthly basis").
Tiền tập 40 bảng + phí đăng ký 20 bảng = Tổng thanh toán ban đầu là 60 bảng.

2. Audio Script toàn văn bài thi Full Exercise
(Các từ khóa dẫn đến đáp án được in đậm)
Receptionist: Good morning, Westlake Sports and Leisure Centre. How can I help you today?
Michael: Hello, I’d like to inquire about joining the club, please.
Receptionist: Certainly! I just need to take down a few details to complete your application. Can I take your name first?
Michael: Yes, it’s Michael Braithwaite.
Receptionist: Could you spell your surname for me, please?
Michael: Sure. It's B-R-A-I-T-H-W-A-I-T-E [Câu 1].
Receptionist: Thank you. And your date of birth, Michael?
Michael: I was born on the 18th of August, 1994 [Câu 2].
Receptionist: Great. Now, what’s the best telephone number to reach you on?
Michael: Well, my home phone is 020 7946 0112, but I'm rarely there during the day. It's much better to use my mobile: 07700 900 452 [Câu 3].
Receptionist: 07700 900 452, got it. And what is your current address?
Michael: I live at number 72, Fairview Avenue, in Kingsford [Câu 4].
Receptionist: Fairview... is that F-A-I-R-V-I-E-W?
Michael: Yes, that's right. And the postcode is KF4 8BL [Câu 5].

Receptionist: Splendid. Now, regarding membership packages, we offer three tiers: Bronze, Silver, and Gold. Gold includes unlimited gym, pool, and racket courts, while Silver excludes personal training sessions.
Michael: I really only need access during off-peak hours and weekends. The Gold sounds a bit excessive for my budget. I think the Silver package suits me best [Câu 6].
Receptionist: Silver it is. What primary sporting facility are you planning to use?
Michael: I enjoy swimming, but my main focus is playing indoor tennis with my partner [Câu 7].
Receptionist: Excellent, we have four brand-new indoor courts. Are there any existing medical conditions or injuries our fitness instructors should know about?
Michael: Nothing serious, though I do have a weak left shoulder from an old rugby injury, so I avoid very heavy lifting [Câu 8].
Receptionist: Understood. Finally, how would you prefer to pay? You can pay an upfront annual fee at a discount, or pay on a monthly direct debit.
Michael: I'd rather spread the expense and pay on a monthly basis, please [Câu 9].
Receptionist: No problem. That will be forty pounds per month, plus an initial registration and security fob fee of twenty pounds, making your total initial payment today exactly 60 pounds [Câu 10].
Michael: Perfect. Here is my credit card.

theory.text: Cẩm nang tự học chuyên sâu & thực hành đề chuẩn Cambridge
I. Theory: Lý thuyết nền tảng & Hệ thống bẫy đề
1. Bản chất & Format Part 2
• Hình thức: Bài nói đơn độc thoại (Monologue) do một người nói duy nhất trình bày trước thính giả hoặc nhóm du khách.

• Bối cảnh: Hướng dẫn, giới thiệu dịch vụ hoặc sự kiện cộng đồng: Hướng dẫn viên du lịch giới thiệu công viên sinh thái, bảo tàng; ban tổ chức thông báo lịch trình lễ hội địa phương; ban quản lý phổ biến quy định trung tâm thể thao.
• Số lượng câu hỏi: 10 câu (Questions 11 – 20).
• Các dạng bài phổ biến nhất:
1. Gắn nhãn Bản đồ / Sơ đồ mặt bằng (Map / Plan Labelling).
2. Câu hỏi trắc nghiệm (Multiple Choice Questions: 1 đáp án A/B/C hoặc chọn 2 trong 5 A–E).
3. Nối thông tin (Matching: Nối địa điểm/dịch vụ với đặc điểm).
• Thách thức lớn nhất: Người nói nói liên tục, không có người thứ hai đối đáp ngắt nhịp; thí sinh dễ bị "lạc đường" trên bản đồ hoặc mắc bẫy trắc nghiệm do cả 3 phương án đều được nhắc tới trong bài.
2. Hệ quy chiếu La bàn, Từ vựng Không gian & Giải phẫu 3 Tầng Bẫy Trắc nghiệm

theory.text: Đồ họa minh họa: Hệ quy chiếu La bàn & 3 Tầng Bẫy Trắc nghiệm Part 2
4 Quy tắc vàng định vị bản đồ:
1. Khóa chặt điểm xuất phát mỏ neo (Starting Anchor Point): Tìm ngay dấu "X" ("You are here") hoặc cổng vào (Main Entrance, South Gate).
2. Phân biệt Hệ quy chiếu La bàn vs Góc nhìn người xem: Có la bàn dùng North/South/East/West; không có la bàn dùng left-hand/right-hand/straight ahead.
3. Bám sát lộ trình di chuyển tuần tự: Thứ tự câu hỏi 11–16 là thứ tự từng bước chân di chuyển của người nói.
4. Nắm chắc từ vựng không gian: adjacent to (sát vách), opposite (đối diện), at the junction/fork (ngã 3), just past (đi qua khỏi), cul-de-sac (đường cụt).

guide.text: II. Guide cách làm bài: Quy trình 4 giai đoạn chuẩn quốc tế
Giai đoạn 1: Pre-listening (Chuẩn bị trước khi nghe)
1. Với bài Bản đồ (Map):
• Đặt ngay đầu bút chì tại vị trí xuất phát ("You are here", Cổng vào).
• Kiểm tra có la bàn không (Bắc - Nam - Đông - Tây hay Trái - Phải).
• Đọc nhanh tên các địa danh đã in sẵn trên bản đồ làm vật mốc (hồ nước, cây cầu, vườn hoa, viện bảo tàng).
2. Với bài Trắc nghiệm (MCQ):
• Đọc kỹ câu hỏi (Question stem) để nắm rõ câu hỏi hỏi về: Nguyên nhân, Mục đích, hay Quy định?
• Gạch chân từ khóa phân biệt sự khác nhau giữa các lựa chọn A, B, C.
Giai đoạn 2: While-listening (Trong khi nghe)

1. Với bài Bản đồ: Rê ngòi bút theo đúng hướng di chuyển của người nói. Khi người nói rẽ trái/phải, di chuyển bút theo con đường đó. Khi nghe thấy từ mốc chỉ vị trí (adjacent to, opposite), khoanh tròn chữ cái tương ứng.
2. Với bài Trắc nghiệm:
• Áp dụng nguyên tắc "Gạch bỏ phương án sai" (Negative Elimination).
• Ngay khi nghe thấy người nói phủ định phương án nào (but that proved unnecessary, cost too much, was cancelled), gạch chéo phương án đó trên đề để giải phóng tầm mắt.
3. Bắt tín hiệu chuyển ý (Signposts): Nghe các từ nối chuyển câu như "Now moving on to...", "Turning now to...", "Next..." để biết người nói đã chuyển sang câu hỏi tiếp theo.
Giai đoạn 3: Post-listening (Rà soát 30 giây)
Kiểm tra xem các câu trả lời dạng chữ cái (A–H) đã điền chính xác, rõ ràng chưa. Không để trống bất kỳ câu nào.
Giai đoạn 4: Post-test Audit (Lập nhật ký lỗi)
Ghi chép lại lỗi: Sai do mất dấu trên bản đồ hay sai do vội vàng chọn ngay đáp án đầu tiên nghe thấy trong câu hỏi trắc nghiệm?

small.text: III. Small Exercises: Bài tập nhỏ rèn micro-skills
E1 · Luyện từ vựng phương hướng & vị trí
Chọn từ thích hợp trong khung điền vào chỗ trống:
Từ khóa: adjacent to • opposite • at the junction • forks • beyond • anticlockwise • cul-de-sac
1. The tourist office is located directly _______________ the museum, on the other side of the central street.
2. The bicycle workshop is _______________ the café, sharing the same brick wall and entrance corridor.
3. Follow the footpath until it _______________ into two separate trails leading up the hillside.
4. The children’s playground is situated right _______________ where North Lane meets Park Avenue.
5. If you walk past the old windmill and continue _______________ the boundary fence, you will reach the orchard.
6. If you tour the animal pens in an _______________ direction, you will start with the sheep pen on your right.
7. Drivers must turn around because the access lane ends in a quiet _______________.

2. Audio Script toàn văn bài thi Full Exercise (Croft Valley Park)
(Các từ khóa dẫn đến đáp án được in đậm)

Park Manager: Good morning everyone and welcome to Croft Valley Park. I'm delighted to see so many visitors here today. Before you set off to explore the grounds, let me orient you using the park map and highlight where everything is located.

Now, if you look at your map, you can see the South Gate at the bottom, where you've all just arrived. The café continues to serve an assortment of drinks and snacks, and it is still in the same place, looking out over the lake and next to the old museum. That's point D on your map [Câu 11: D].

We’re hoping to change the location of the toilets, and bring them nearer to the centre of the park as they’re a bit out of the way at present, near the adventure playground, in the far corner of your map at point C [Câu 12: C].

As for the formal gardens, they used to be behind the old museum, but now you can find them in the space near the south gate, between the park boundary and the path that goes past the lake towards the museum. That's location G [Câu 13: G].

We've also set up a brand-new outdoor gym. You have to look for it as it's a bit hidden in the trees, but it's right next to the glass houses, just to the right of the path as you enter from the south gate. That's area H [Câu 14: H].

One very successful introduction has been our skateboard ramp. It's near the old museum, at the end of a little path that leads off from the main path between the lake and the museum, up at point A [Câu 15: A].

Then we have the area for wild flowers, which has been extended recently. If you walk north from the lake, past the adventure playground, you’ll see them right up in that top-left area marked E [Câu 16: E].
Now let me tell you a bit more about some of the changes and visitor regulations at Croft Valley Park.

First, our adventure playground. We were aware that we had nowhere for children to let off steam, and decided to use our municipal funding to construct a completely new facility in a large space to the north of the park. It's open year-round, and entrance is completely free [Câu 17/18: D]. However, for safety reasons, we do insist that all young children must be accompanied and supervised by a responsible adult at all times [Câu 17/18: A].

As for our new skate park and skateboard ramp, please note that while it is free of charge, all users must wear approved safety helmets and knee pads [Câu 19/20: A]. Anyone found riding without safety gear will be asked to leave by our park rangers.

Finally, regarding our glass houses, they feature rare tropical plants, so we keep them at a strictly regulated temperature. Photography with flash is strictly prohibited inside the glass houses [Câu 19/20: C], and dogs are not allowed inside under any circumstances. Thank you for your attention, and enjoy your visit to Croft Valley Park!

I. Theory: Lý thuyết nền tảng & Bẫy thảo luận nhóm
1. Bản chất & Format Part 3
• Hình thức: Cuộc thảo luận học thuật giữa 2 đến 4 người (Conversation / Group Discussion).
• Bối cảnh: Môi trường đại học và học thuật (Academic & Educational context):
• Hai sinh viên thảo luận về bài tập nhóm, bài nghiên cứu thực địa, hoặc bài thuyết trình hội thảo.
• Sinh viên gặp giáo sư/giảng viên hướng dẫn (Tutor / Academic Supervisor) để nhận phản hồi và góp ý cho đề tài luận văn.
• Số lượng câu hỏi: 10 câu (Questions 21 – 30).
• Dạng câu hỏi chủ đạo:
1. Trắc nghiệm nhiều lựa chọn (Multiple Choice dài: 1 đáp án A/B/C hoặc chọn 2 trong 5).
2. Nối thông tin phân công nhiệm vụ / đánh giá tiêu chí (Matching tasks / Classification).
3. Hoàn thành lưu đồ quy trình nghiên cứu (Flow-chart completion).

3 Bẫy kinh điển cần ghi nhớ:
1. Phân biệt chủ thể câu hỏi (Speaker Voice): Để ý câu hỏi hỏi về ý kiến của ai (Jack, Emma, hay Giáo sư). Đừng vội khoanh ý của người đầu tiên phát biểu.
2. Bẫy xoay chiều & Thỏa hiệp (Compromise Trap): Người nói thường trải qua: Đề xuất ban đầu (Bị phản bác) ➔ Khó khăn/Rào cản ➔ Thỏa hiệp cuối cùng. Đáp án đúng luôn là quyết định thỏa hiệp cuối cùng.
3. Kỹ thuật Paraphrase học thuật: Từ ngữ trong bài nghe được diễn đạt bằng các thuật ngữ tương đương (ví dụ: oversaturated data = already far too much existing research).

guide.text: II. Guide cách làm bài: Quy trình 4 giai đoạn chuẩn quốc tế
Giai đoạn 1: Pre-listening (Tận dụng 30–45 giây trước khi nghe)
1. Xác định rõ CHỦ THỂ câu hỏi:
• Đọc lướt câu hỏi và khoanh tròn ngay đối tượng: Đề đang hỏi về ý kiến của Jack, Emma, hay Cả hai người (Both), hay Tutor?
2. Gạch chân từ khóa nội dung (Content Keywords):
• Trong câu hỏi trắc nghiệm dài, đừng cố dịch từng chữ. Hãy gạch chân 1–2 danh từ/động từ chính tạo nên sự khác biệt giữa các phương án A, B, C.
3. Với bài Nối nhiệm vụ (Matching):
• Đọc lướt danh sách công việc (A–F) để nắm nhanh các ý tưởng chính (lập bảng số liệu, chụp ảnh, phỏng vấn...).
Giai đoạn 2: While-listening (Trong khi nghe)
1. Phân biệt ngay chất giọng các nhân vật:
• Xác định ai là giọng nam (Jack), ai là giọng nữ (Emma), ai là giọng lớn tuổi hơn/học thuật hơn (Giáo sư).
2. Không vội chọn ngay khi mới nghe người đầu tiên phát biểu:
• Hãy lắng nghe phản hồi của người đối thoại. Chờ đợi từ nối phản bác (but, however, although) hoặc từ đồng thuận (agreed, fair enough).
3. Bắt nhịp chốt thỏa hiệp:
• Đáp án đúng luôn nằm ở kết luận cuối cùng mà các nhân vật đồng thuận thực hiện.
Giai đoạn 3: Post-listening (Rà soát 30 giây)
Kiểm tra xem bạn có khoanh nhầm câu hỏi phân công cá nhân hay không (ví dụ đề hỏi Jack làm gì mà lại khoanh việc của Emma).
Giai đoạn 4: Post-test Audit (Lập nhật ký lỗi)
Ghi chép: Sai do nhầm người nói, do vội vàng chọn đề xuất ban đầu bị hủy, hay do không nhận ra cặp từ đồng nghĩa (paraphrase)?

2. Audio Script toàn văn bài thi Full Exercise
(Các từ khóa dẫn đến đáp án được in đậm)
Professor Henderson: Come in, Jack, Emma. Take a seat. How are your preparations coming along for next month's marine biodiversity project?
Emma: Well, Professor Henderson, we've reviewed the three potential survey locations along the southern coastline. We originally favored St. Peter's Bay because of its large seal colony.

Jack: Yes, and Rocky Cove has that fascinating tidal rock pool ecosystem, but tourist boats disturb the area too frequently. So we both agreed that Blackwood Estuary would provide the most reliable, undisturbed sample site for our research [Câu 21].
Professor Henderson: A sensible choice, Blackwood Estuary has strict conservation protection. Now, what about your core research methodology?

Jack: We initially planned to collect water samples at various depths to test salinity and oxygen levels. But after reading last year's research papers, we realized that analyzing macro-invertebrate population density gives a much more accurate picture of ecological health [Câu 22].
Emma: Exactly, macro-invertebrates act as bio-indicators over long periods, whereas dissolved oxygen fluctuates hour by hour.
Professor Henderson: Good thinking. Have you sorted out your equipment needs with the laboratory technician?

Emma: Most items are ready, like the collection nets and chemical testing kits. However, we ran into an issue with the underwater digital cameras. The department only has two waterproof enclosures left, and both are currently reserved by the postgraduates [Câu 23].
Jack: So instead of underwater video recording, we'll be using hand-drawn quadrant grid frames to record species distribution manually from the shore.
Professor Henderson: That's perfectly acceptable for undergraduate fieldwork. And how will you record your field measurements in wet conditions?

Jack: We thought about using waterproof tablets, but batteries drain rapidly in cold sea air. Emma suggested using waterproof synthetic paper notebooks with pencil, and entering the data into our spreadsheet software each evening at the hostel.
Emma: It guarantees we won't lose raw data in the field due to battery failure [Câu 24].
Professor Henderson: Very prudent. Now, before university ethics approval is granted, you must address one potential hazard: handling wild marine organisms.

Jack: Yes, we’ve included a strict catch-and-release protocol. Any crabs or small fish will be kept in aerated seawater buckets for no longer than fifteen minutes before being safely returned to the exact pool where they were found [Câu 25].
Professor Henderson: Splendid. Now let's look at the division of responsibilities between you two.

Jack: Well, for the environmental baseline measurements—specifically measuring water temperature and pH levels across all six stations—I will take care of that, as I'm familiar with the digital probes [Câu 26: Jack].
Emma: And I’ll handle the specimen identification and microscopic taxonomy in the mobile lab, using the reference handbook [Câu 27: Emma].

Jack: When it comes to compiling the statistical regression models and producing the correlation graphs, Emma is much better at R programming than I am, so she volunteered to take the lead on that [Câu 28: Emma].

Emma: That's right. But for conducting interviews with the local inshore fishermen to record their observations over the past decade, Jack is going to do that, since his uncle is part of the local harbor association and knows the skippers personally [Câu 29: Jack].
Jack: And finally, we’ll design the final academic presentation slides together, ensuring our conclusions are clearly structured for the symposium [Câu 30: Both].
Professor Henderson: Excellent teamwork. I'll sign off your project proposal right away.

2. Bám chặt biển chỉ đường (Lecture Signposts):
• "To begin with...": Mở đầu phần 1.
• "Now, turning our attention to...": Báo hiệu chuyển sang tiêu đề lớn tiếp theo.
• "Consequently...": Trình bày kết quả / hệ quả.
• "By contrast...": So sánh tương phản.

3. Quy tắc rút trực tiếp từ gốc (Direct Word Extraction): Không tự ý biến đổi dạng từ. Kiểm tra kỹ tính hòa hợp ngữ pháp và đuôi danh từ số nhiều -s/-es.

guide.text: II. Guide cách làm bài: Quy trình 4 giai đoạn chuẩn quốc tế
Giai đoạn 1: Pre-listening (Chiến thuật 60–90 giây vàng ngọc)
1. Quét toàn bộ cấu trúc bài giảng từ câu 31 đến 40:
• Đọc nhanh các tiêu đề in đậm (Headings) để nắm khung sườn nội dung.
2. Kỹ thuật "Mỏ neo ngữ pháp" (Grammatical Anchor):
• Xác định từ loại cần điền cho từng chỗ trống:
• Đứng sau tính từ -> Cần một Danh từ (massive central ventilation [ 32 ] -> Cần danh từ).
• Đứng sau mạo từ a/an -> Cần Danh từ số ít đếm được.
• Đứng sau động từ chỉ hành vi -> Cần Danh từ/Tân ngữ.
3. Dự đoán trường nghĩa: Chỗ trống này nói về vật liệu, con vật, căn phòng, hay hiện tượng tự nhiên?
Giai đoạn 2: While-listening (Trong khi nghe)
1. Kỹ thuật "Mắt trước tai một nhịp" (Eye-ear coordination):
• Đây là kỹ năng sống còn của Part 4: Khi tai đang nghe thông tin của câu 32, mắt PHẢI LIẾC XUỐNG câu 33 và 34.
• Nếu bạn chỉ nhìn chăm chăm vào câu 32, khi băng nói lướt qua bạn sẽ bị lỡ luôn câu 33 và 34 mà không hề hay biết.
2. Bám chặt biển chỉ đường (Signposts):
• Nghe thấy giảng viên đổi giọng hoặc dùng từ chuyển đoạn ("Now, turning our attention to...") là biết bài đã chuyển sang tiêu đề lớn tiếp theo.
3. Bắt đúng từ gốc trong bài nghe:
• Không tự ý biến đổi dạng từ (ví dụ băng nói temperature thì không tự sửa thành temperatures).
Giai đoạn 3: Post-listening (Rà soát 1 phút cuối)
1. Kiểm tra tính hòa hợp ngữ pháp: Đọc lại cả câu ghi chú xem từ vừa điền có tạo thành một câu hoàn chỉnh, đúng ngữ pháp tiếng Anh không.
2. Kiểm tra đuôi số nhiều `-s/-es`: Nhìn lại danh từ xem có mạo từ không, nếu là danh từ đếm được đứng một mình thì bắt buộc phải có -s.
Giai đoạn 4: Post-test Audit (Lập nhật ký lỗi)
Ghi chép: Sai do bị "trôi băng" (không kịp nhìn câu tiếp theo), do sai chính tả từ học thuật, hay do thừa/thiếu âm đuôi -s?

2. Audio Script toàn văn bài thi Full Exercise
(Các từ khóa dẫn đến đáp án được in đậm)

Professor William Hughes: Good morning, everyone. In today’s lecture on architectural history and sustainable urbanism, we will explore an extraordinary human achievement: the subterranean settlements of ancient times, with a particular focus on Derinkuyu in Cappadocia, modern-day Turkey. We will also examine how the engineering principles behind these ancient cities are inspiring twenty-first-century urban architects facing severe land shortages and climate extremes.

To begin with, let us look at the geological foundation. Derinkuyu was carved directly out of thick layers of volcanic ash known as tufa. This stone possessed a unique characteristic: it was exceptionally soft [Câu 31] when freshly excavated, allowing inhabitants to hollow out extensive subterranean chambers using simple bronze and iron chisels. However, once exposed to air, the rock hardened remarkably, providing immense structural stability without requiring wooden support beams.

Now, how did thousands of people survive deep beneath the earth for months at a time during enemy sieges? The foremost engineering priority was airflow. The architects constructed massive central ventilation shafts [Câu 32], some descending over fifty-five meters deep. These shafts acted as giant chimneys, pulling cool, fresh air from the surface down to the lowest eighth floor, while warm, stale air was naturally expelled upward through narrow secondary ducts.

Equally ingenious was the city’s defense system. If foreign invaders managed to penetrate the surface entrance, the inhabitants could roll massive disc-shaped stone doors [Câu 33] across the corridors. These doors, weighing up to five hundred kilograms each, could only be operated from the inside and featured a central hole through which defenders could thrust spears [Câu 34] at attackers.

In terms of internal organization, the city was meticulously zoned. The uppermost levels directly below the surface were reserved for domestic livestock [Câu 35], such as goats and cattle. This prevented heavy animals from traversing steep downward stairs, while animal body heat provided natural warmth for the living quarters situated immediately below. Further down were community dining halls, oil presses, wineries, and even a large vaulted religious school [Câu 36].
Now, let us turn our attention to the present day. Why are contemporary civil engineers and urban planners looking underground once again?

The first major advantage is thermal insulation. Below a depth of just five meters, the earth maintains a virtually constant temperature [Câu 37] throughout the entire year, typically between fifteen and eighteen degrees Celsius. Subterranean buildings therefore require minimal artificial heating in winter and negligible air conditioning in summer, drastically reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

A second compelling benefit is acoustic insulation. Dense earth and rock serve as an impenetrable acoustic barrier, effectively eliminating environmental noise [Câu 38] pollution caused by surface highways, railway lines, and flight paths. This makes underground spaces ideal for libraries, server farms, research laboratories, and residential developments in hyper-dense metropolises like Tokyo or Singapore.

Furthermore, subterranean structures possess exceptional structural resilience against natural hazards. Above-ground skyscrapers sway violently during tectonic tremors and are vulnerable to typhoons, whereas underground complexes move in harmony with the surrounding rock mass, suffering remarkably less seismic [Câu 39] damage during major earthquakes.

Finally, moving infrastructure underground preserves our most precious surface resource: fertile agricultural soil [Câu 40] and natural biodiverse habitats. By burying transport networks, shopping complexes, and energy generation deep below, surface land can be re-wilded or reserved exclusively for sustainable food cultivation and public parks. In short, ancient subterranean architecture offers profound lessons for the resilient cities of tomorrow. Thank you for your attention.

theory.text: IELTS SPEAKING
Part 1
A step-by-step self-study guide
Understand the interview • Build natural answers • Practise short skills • Plan ideas • Complete full practice sets
This guide focuses on IELTS Speaking Part 1: the introductory interview about familiar topics such as home, study, work, daily routines, interests and preferences.
Your learning route

rows: Learn the task format, answer development, fluency, vocabulary and grammar.
Use the worked examples as reference.
Practise extending answers, choosing details, paraphrasing and correcting common errors.
Exercises E1–E9; keys at the end.
Make quick keyword plans for familiar topics without writing full answers.
Planning worksheets P1–P10; suggested plans at the end.
Answer complete sets aloud under realistic timing, then review your recording.
Compare with sample answers, explanations and self-review checklists.
All keys and sample responses are at the end.

theory.text: A study routine you can repeat

Session 1: Read one theory section and say the worked examples aloud. Session 2: Complete two or three small exercises. Session 3: plan two topics using keywords, then answer them without reading a script. Session 4: record one full practice set, review it and repeat the weakest answers.

Start untimed. Later, aim to answer each question in roughly 2–4 sentences when the question invites development. This is a practice guide, not an official requirement for a fixed number of sentences or seconds. The examiner may move on naturally; do not force every answer to the same length.

Important: sample answers are examples, not scripts to memorise. Replace the details with truthful information about your own life. IELTS assesses how you communicate in the interview, not whether your life matches the model answer.
Part 1 Theory
1. Understand the task

IELTS Speaking has three parts. Part 1 is a short interview in which the examiner asks questions about familiar topics. It normally lasts about 4–5 minutes. The questions are designed to let you talk about your life, habits, preferences and everyday experiences.

rows: What it means for your answer
Use real experiences and ordinary details; you do not need specialist knowledge.
Answer the question directly before adding a reason, detail or example.
Listen to the exact wording. A question about the past may need a past-tense answer.
Aim for clear, natural communication rather than an essay-like response.
No preparation time for each question
Develop the habit of thinking of one useful detail quickly.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Question: “Do you enjoy cooking?” A direct answer could be: “Yes, quite a lot.” A developed answer is: “Yes, quite a lot. I usually cook simple dishes at home, especially on weekends, because it helps me relax and saves money.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The answer responds immediately, then adds a routine and a reason. It does not begin with a long general statement about the importance of cooking. The details are specific enough to sound personal but easy to say.
2. Use a flexible answer pattern

A useful starting pattern is A–R–D: Answer → Reason → Detail. Add an example or contrast only when it helps. This is a planning aid, not a compulsory formula; natural answers may use two steps or reorder them.

rows: Give a clear response to the question.
Yes, usually. / Not really. / It depends. / I’d say…
mainly because… / one reason is that… / I suppose it’s because…
Add a real routine, example, place, person or contrast.
For example… / especially when… / These days… / Unlike before…

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Question: “Do you like reading?” Answer: “Yes, especially short non-fiction books. I like learning something practical without spending too much time on it, so I often read a few pages before bed.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Answer: yes. Reason: practical learning. Detail: short reading before bed. Each sentence adds information instead of repeating “I like reading because it is interesting.”
3. Choose the right amount of detail

A one-word answer may be understandable but gives you little opportunity to show fluency, vocabulary or grammar. At the other extreme, a long monologue can drift away from the question and create more chances for errors. A practical target is a direct answer plus one or two relevant supporting details.

rows: “Yes, I do. I usually walk in the evening because it clears my head after studying.”
“Yes, walking is important in human civilisation, and throughout history…”

theory.text: Do not add a reason when it feels unnatural or when the question simply asks for a factual detail. For “What is your hometown called?”, name the place and perhaps add a brief description. For “Why do you like it?”, explain the reason.
4. Answer the exact question

rows: Give a yes/no or qualified answer, then develop it.
Name a type or category, then give a detail.
Giving only a reason without naming anything.
State frequency, then describe a routine.
Answering only whether you enjoy it.
Give a time or period, then explain if useful.
Giving a general opinion without a time.
Name a place and describe it briefly.
Talking only about why the activity matters.
Give a reason and make it clear.
Repeating the question as the whole answer.
Talk about the past using appropriate tense.
Using present tense for a finished past experience.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Q: “How often do you use public transport?” Weak: “It’s convenient and cheap.” Better: “I use it several times a week, mainly when I go to university. It’s cheaper than taking a taxi, and I don’t have to find a parking space.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The improved answer begins with frequency, which is what “how often” asks for. The reasons support the answer rather than replacing it.
5. Sound natural: spoken English, not an essay

Part 1 answers should sound like thoughtful conversation. Contractions such as “I’m”, “it’s” and “don’t” are normal. Simple language is effective when it is precise. Avoid memorised openings such as “Since the dawn of time…” or “This is an intriguing question that requires deep consideration.”

rows: I think… / I’d say… / For me,…
In my humble opinion… (often overly formal)
usually / probably / more or less / I guess
Maybe, perhaps, possibly in every sentence
A long list of unrelated examples
I used to…, but these days…
Mixing past and present without a clear time change
It depends on… / If I have time,…
Using “it depends” without explaining what it depends on

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Q: “Do you often go to cafés?” Natural: “Not that often. I usually meet friends at a café once or twice a month, especially when we want somewhere quiet to chat.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Not that often” is a natural qualified answer. The frequency and situation clarify what it means. The answer is conversational without being careless.
6. Develop vocabulary through specific details

You do not need rare words for familiar topics. Choose words that describe your experience accurately. A small, useful phrase such as “a quiet neighbourhood”, “a packed schedule”, “a short commute” or “a relaxing way to unwind” can be more effective than an unnatural advanced synonym.

rows: a residential area; within walking distance; a lively neighbourhood
“I live in a fairly quiet residential area.”
meet a deadline; a practical subject; a heavy workload
“The workload gets heavy near exam week.”
unwind after class; take up a hobby; spend time outdoors
“I go cycling to unwind after class.”
keep in touch; look something up; spend time on a screen
“I use my phone to keep in touch with friends.”
home-cooked meals; a balanced diet; grab a quick bite
“I often have home-cooked meals on weekdays.”
rush-hour traffic; a reliable service; get around town
“Buses make it easier to get around town.”

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Basic: “My area is good and has many things.” More precise: “My neighbourhood is convenient because there are several cafés and grocery stores within walking distance.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Convenient” summarises the benefit, while “within walking distance” gives a concrete reason. The goal is precision, not decoration.
7. Use grammar that matches the meaning

rows: “I’m preparing for my final exams at the moment.”
“I joined a photography club last year.”
“I used to play badminton every weekend.”
be going to / plan to / hope to
“I’m planning to learn how to drive.”
usually, often, once a week, hardly ever
“I go swimming about once a week.”
prefer A to B; would rather + verb
“I prefer studying in the morning to studying late at night.”

theory.text: A useful answer can contain more than one tense when the time changes: “I used to live in a small town, but I moved to the city three years ago, and I’m much busier now.” Make the timeline clear.
8. Fluency: keep going without rushing

Fluency is not the same as speaking as fast as possible. It includes connecting ideas, maintaining a manageable pace and recovering when you need a moment to think. A brief pause is fine. Repeatedly restarting the entire sentence, filling every silence with “umm”, or speaking so quickly that words become unclear can make communication harder.
Think of one key idea, not a complete memorised sentence.
Use a short thinking phrase only when needed: “Let me think…” or “I’d say…”.
If you lose a word, explain it another way: “It’s a device you use to…”
Finish the point when you have answered the question; do not keep adding unrelated ideas.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Q: “What do you usually do at weekends?” If you cannot recall a specific activity immediately: “It depends on my workload. If I’m free, I usually meet a friend or watch a film at home. During exam periods, I tend to stay in and study.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “It depends on…” gives a clear organising idea, and the two contrasting situations make the answer easy to follow.
9. Pronunciation: clarity first

Aim for intelligible speech, clear word endings and natural stress. You do not need to imitate a particular accent. Practise saying key content words clearly and grouping words into meaningful chunks. For example: “I usually take the BUS / because it’s CHEAPER / and more CONVENIENT.” Do not pause after every word.
Record yourself and check whether important words are easy to hear.
Practise word stress in useful phrases: con-VEN-ient, neigh-bour-HOOD, en-vi-ron-MENT.
Notice final sounds and plural endings: “books”, “friends”, “worked”.
Repeat a short answer with clearer chunking rather than simply speaking faster.
10. Handle common Part 1 topics
Part 1 often uses everyday topics. Prepare flexible vocabulary and real details rather than memorising a paragraph for each possible question.

rows: Where do you live? What do you like about your home? Which room do you use most?
What is your hometown like? What has changed? Would you recommend visiting it?
What do you study or do? Why did you choose it? What do you find challenging?
What is a typical day like? Are your routines different at weekends?
What do you do to relax? Did you have the same hobbies as a child?
What kind of food do you like? Do you cook? Has your diet changed?

theory.text: 11. Assessment criteria in practical terms

IELTS Speaking is assessed across four criteria: Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation. You do not need to show every feature in every answer. Across the interview, aim to communicate clearly, connect ideas, use suitable vocabulary, vary grammar where natural and make your speech easy to understand.

rows: Answer without excessive hesitation; organise the response; avoid repetition and irrelevant detail.
Use accurate topic words and collocations; paraphrase when a word is missing; avoid forced idioms.
Control basic sentences and add a range of clauses and tenses where they fit.
Make sounds, word stress and sentence stress clear; use natural chunking and a manageable pace.

theory.text: These are study explanations, not a band-score calculator. A single answer cannot reliably determine your overall Speaking band.
12. A 10-second mental checklist
Did I answer the exact question first?
Did I add one relevant reason, detail or example?
Does my tense match the time in the question?
Are my words specific and natural?
Can the listener follow my speech without effort?

guide.text: Part 3 Planning guide

The aim is to plan ideas, not to write a memorised speech. For each question, note only two or three keywords: your answer, one reason, and one detail. Then look away from the notes and speak naturally.
A reusable 15-second planning worksheet

rows: Yes / no / sometimes / it depends / a specific fact: ______________________________
when / where / who with / example / past-versus-now: ______________________________
Present habit / past experience / future plan / frequency: __________________________
A precise collocation or phrase I can use naturally: ________________________________

guide.text: A worked planning example
Question: “Do you enjoy taking photos?”

rows: photos of food / scenery; share with friends

guide.text: Possible spoken answer: “Yes, especially when I travel. I like taking photos because they help me capture a moment and remember the place later. I usually take pictures of scenery or food and share a few with my friends.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The notes are not complete sentences. That is intentional: they give the speaker a direction without encouraging recitation. The final answer uses connected sentences and adds grammar spontaneously.

small.text: Part 2 Small exercises
Complete these tasks before checking the answer key. Say your answers aloud when the task involves speaking. The suggested times are practice estimates, not official IELTS timings.
E1. Extend a short answer
Allow 6 minutes. Add a reason and one specific detail to each answer. Do not write more than two additional sentences.
1. Q: Do you like your hometown? A: Yes, I do. →
2. Q: How often do you exercise? A: About twice a week. →
3. Q: Do you enjoy cooking? A: Not really. →
4. Q: What do you do in your free time? A: I watch films. →
5. Q: Do you use your phone a lot? A: Yes, quite a lot. →
E2. Match the answer to the question
Allow 4 minutes. Write the correct question number beside each answer.
Questions: (1) How often do you read? (2) What kind of music do you like? (3) Where do you usually study? (4) Did you enjoy sports at school? (5) Why do you use public transport?

A. “Mostly pop and acoustic music, especially when I’m travelling.”B. “Because it’s affordable, and I can avoid looking for a parking space.”C. “Usually in the library, since it’s quieter than my room.”D. “A few times a week, usually before I go to bed.”E. “Yes, I did. I played volleyball with my classmates for two years.”
E3. Improve the answer
Allow 8 minutes. Rewrite each answer so that it answers the question directly and includes relevant detail.
1. Q: How do you get to university? A: “Transport is very important in modern society.”
2. Q: What do you like about your neighbourhood? A: “It is good. It is very good and nice.”
3. Q: Did you enjoy reading as a child? A: “I like reading fantasy books now.”
4. Q: How often do you eat out? A: “Restaurants have many kinds of food, and food is necessary.”
E4. Choose precise vocabulary
Allow 5 minutes. Complete each sentence with the most suitable phrase: within walking distance • unwind • packed schedule • keep in touch • rush-hour traffic.
1. My weekdays are busy because I have a __________.
2. I usually listen to music to __________ after class.
3. There are several shops __________ of my apartment.
4. Messaging apps help me __________ with friends who live far away.
5. I leave home early to avoid the worst __________.
E5. Correct the grammar
Allow 8 minutes. Correct the error and briefly name the grammar point.
1. I am usually go to university by bus.
2. I have joined a club last year.
3. I prefer study in the morning than at night.
4. When I was a child, I use to play outside every day.
5. I enjoy to watch films with my friends.
E6. Use the right tense
Allow 6 minutes. Complete each answer using the verb in brackets.
1. Q: What do you do at weekends? A: I usually __________ (meet) friends or __________ (stay) at home.
2. Q: Did you like your school? A: Yes. I __________ (make) a lot of friends there.
3. Q: Are you learning anything new at the moment? A: I __________ (try) to improve my English pronunciation.
4. Q: Have your hobbies changed? A: I __________ (play) computer games a lot as a teenager, but now I __________ (prefer) outdoor activities.
5. Q: What are your plans for next year? A: I __________ (hope) to take an English test.
E7. Build a natural response
Allow 8 minutes. Choose one connector from the box for each gap: especially • although • so • for example • these days.
1. I like outdoor activities, __________ cycling and walking.
2. I’m quite busy with university, __________ I try to exercise at weekends.
3. I enjoy cooking, __________ when I have time to try a new recipe.
4. I used to watch television every evening. __________, I mostly watch videos online.
5. I like my neighbourhood, __________ I try to spend time outdoors.
E8. Recover when you do not know a word
Allow 6 minutes. Explain the underlined idea without using the word itself. Aim for one or two sentences.
1. “I use a thermos to keep my drink warm.” Explain what a thermos is.
2. “I enjoy gardening because it helps me relax.” Explain what gardening means.
3. “I take the underground train to work when traffic is heavy.” Explain what an underground train is.
4. “I watched a documentary about ocean life last night.” Explain what a documentary is.
E9. Spot the problem
Allow 6 minutes. Identify the main weakness in each response: off-topic, too short, repetitive, memorised/formal, or tense mismatch. Then state one improvement.
1. Q: What do you usually do after class? A: “Yes.”
2. Q: What is your hometown like? A: “My hometown is nice. It is really nice, and I think it is a nice place.”
3. Q: Did you play any sports when you were younger? A: “I play badminton every Sunday.”
4. Q: Do you enjoy shopping? A: “Since the dawn of civilisation, shopping has been a fundamental pillar of human existence.”
5. Q: How often do you cook? A: “Food is important because all humans need nutrition.”

review.text: Part 5 Complete answer key
The answers below are suggestions. Many different responses are correct if they answer the question, use appropriate grammar and sound natural. Personalise every model before practising it aloud.
Answers for E1: Extend a short answer
1. Hometown: Yes, I do. I like that it has plenty of food stalls and cafés, and most places I need are easy to reach.
2. Exercise: I exercise about twice a week, usually by cycling or doing a short workout at home. It helps me stay active when I have a lot of coursework.
3. Cooking: Not really. I can make a few simple dishes, but I usually choose meals that do not take long to prepare.
4. Free time: I watch films, especially comedies. It is an easy way to relax after studying, and sometimes I watch them with friends.
5. Phone: Yes, quite a lot. I use it to message friends, check my timetable and look up information for my classes.
Answers for E2: Match the answer
A–2; B–5; C–3; D–1; E–4. Each answer matches the information requested by its question: type, reason, location, frequency or past experience.
Answers for E3: Improve the answer
1. “I usually take the bus to university because it is affordable and the stop is close to my home.” It answers how and adds a reason.
2. “I like that my neighbourhood is quiet, and there are several grocery stores within walking distance.” It replaces vague repetition with specific detail.
3. “Yes, I did. I used to read fantasy books before bed, although I mostly read online articles now.” The answer uses past tense and can contrast with the present.
4. “I eat out about once a week, usually at the weekend when I meet friends. On weekdays, I tend to eat at home.” It answers frequency first.
Answers for E4: Precise vocabulary
1. packed schedule; 2. unwind; 3. within walking distance; 4. keep in touch; 5. rush-hour traffic.
Answers for E5: Grammar correction
1. “I usually go to university by bus.” Present simple for a routine; do not combine “am” with the base verb this way.
2. “I joined a club last year.” The finished time “last year” normally takes the past simple.
3. “I prefer studying in the morning to studying at night.” Use prefer + -ing + to + -ing, or “prefer to study … rather than …”.
4. “When I was a child, I used to play outside every day.” The expression is “used to + base verb” for a past habit.
5. “I enjoy watching films with my friends.” Use enjoy + -ing.
Answers for E6: Use the right tense
1. meet; stay. 2. made. 3. am trying. 4. played; prefer. 5. hope (or “am hoping” in a suitable context). The tense follows the time and meaning in the question.
Answers for E7: Natural response
1. for example; 2. although; 3. especially; 4. These days; 5. so. Use “especially” to single out one item or situation, not to show contrast.
Answers for E8: Explain without the word
1. “It is a container that keeps drinks hot or cold for a long time.”
2. “It means growing and looking after plants, flowers or vegetables.”
3. “It is an underground train system used to travel around a city.”
4. “It is a programme that gives factual information about real people, places, events or subjects.”
Answers for E9: Spot the problem
1. Too short / does not answer the question. Give one or two usual activities, such as having a snack or reviewing notes.
2. Repetitive and vague. Replace repeated “nice” with a concrete feature and a reason.
3. Tense mismatch. The question asks about the past; use “I played…” or “I used to play…”.
4. Memorised or overly formal. Give a direct personal answer, e.g. “Yes, especially when I need clothes or books.”
5. Off-topic. Explain how often you cook and add a routine or reason.
Suggested plans for P1–P10
P1 Home: apartment / quiet / favourite room = bedroom or study corner / future: larger place or stay nearby
P2 Hometown: city or town name / food and familiar places / new roads or buildings / visitor: local market or park
P3 Study / work: subject / reason: interest or career / challenge: workload or difficult concepts / study routine
P4 Routine: wake-up time / breakfast / commute / weekend: later start or social plans
P5 Free time: music, films, sport or games / reason: relax / prefer alone or with friends / future hobby
P6 Food: favourite dish / taste or memory / cook simple meals / diet changed because of schedule or health goals
P7 Friends: weekly or monthly / café, meal or online game / making friends: shared interests / close friends versus larger circle
P8 Technology: phone or laptop / study, messages, navigation / saves time / drawback: distraction
P9 Transport: bus, motorbike, walking or cycling / cost and convenience / service quality / improve routes or reliability
P10 Childhood: outdoor games, drawing, reading / who with / changed due to school or work / current hobby
These are keyword examples only. Your plan should reflect your own life; there is no single correct personal answer.
Model answers for full practice sets
The following models demonstrate answer length and development. They are not full scripts for memorisation. If a model does not match your circumstances, change the details.
F1. Home and accommodation
Q1 model: “I live in an apartment with my family. It is in a fairly convenient area, so shops and public transport are not too far away.”
Q2 model: “My favourite thing is that it feels comfortable and familiar. After a long day at university, it is nice to have somewhere quiet to relax.”
Q3 model: “I spend most of my time in my bedroom because I study there and keep my books and computer there. I have a small desk near the window.”
Q4 model: “Possibly. I would like to try living closer to the city centre for a while, mainly because it would make travelling around easier. However, I would still want a quiet place.”
F2. Hometown
Q1 model: “My hometown is in southern Vietnam. It is a fairly busy place, but there are also quieter residential areas.”
Q2 model: “I like the food and the fact that most people are familiar with the area. There are plenty of local places to eat, and I can usually find what I need nearby.”
Q3 model: “Yes, quite a bit. There are more shops and newer buildings than there used to be, although some older neighbourhoods have stayed much the same.”
Q4 model: “Yes, especially for someone who enjoys local food and everyday city life. I would suggest visiting a local market and trying a few regional dishes.”
F3. Study
Q1 model: “I’m studying computer engineering. It combines programming with hardware, which is what attracted me to it.”
Q2 model: “I chose it because I enjoy understanding how devices work and how software can interact with physical systems. It also gives me several possible career paths.”
Q3 model: “The most difficult part is managing several technical subjects at once. Some concepts take time to understand, so I try to practise them rather than only read notes.”
Q4 model: “I usually review the main concepts first and then solve practice questions. If I get something wrong, I try to understand why before moving to the next topic.”
F4. Daily routine
Q1 model: “I usually get up, have breakfast and check what I need to do that day. If I have an early class, I try to leave home with enough time for the journey.”
Q2 model: “I like having a rough routine because it helps me manage my time, but I do not plan every minute. I need some flexibility when assignments take longer than expected.”
Q3 model: “At weekends, I usually wake up later and have more time for hobbies or friends. During the week, most of my time is taken up by classes and coursework.”
Q4 model: “I would like to spend less time on my phone before bed. I sometimes keep scrolling longer than I intend to, so I’m trying to put it away earlier.”
F5. Free time and hobbies
Q1 model: “I usually watch films, listen to music or work on a personal project. It depends on how much coursework I have that week.”
Q2 model: “Not exactly. When I was younger, I spent more time playing games outdoors. These days, I have more screen-based hobbies, although I still enjoy going out.”
Q3 model: “I enjoy both, but it depends on the activity. I prefer doing exercise with other people, while I often watch films or study a hobby on my own.”
Q4 model: “I’d like to try photography properly. I take pictures on my phone already, but I want to learn more about composition and lighting.”
F6. Food and cooking
Q1 model: “I enjoy Vietnamese food, particularly dishes with fresh herbs and a balance of different flavours. I also like trying food from other countries when I get the chance.”
Q2 model: “I usually eat at home on weekdays because it is more affordable and convenient. I eat out when I meet friends or want to try somewhere new.”
Q3 model: “I can cook a few simple meals, such as fried rice or noodles. I’m not particularly skilled, but I can prepare something decent when I need to.”
Q4 model: “My eating habits have changed a little. I used to snack more often, but now I try to eat proper meals, especially when I have a busy study schedule.”
F7. Friends
Q1 model: “I meet my friends whenever our schedules allow, usually once a week or so. Sometimes we meet in person, and sometimes we just chat online.”
Q2 model: “We often get something to eat, visit a café or play games together. It is usually more about catching up than doing anything special.”
Q3 model: “I think it becomes easier when we have something in common, such as a class or hobby. I can be a little quiet at first, but I get more comfortable after a while.”
Q4 model: “I prefer a few close friends because I find it easier to talk openly with them. That said, it is also nice to know people from different backgrounds.”
F8. Technology
Q1 model: “I probably use my laptop the most for studying, although my phone is the device I carry everywhere. I use both almost every day.”
Q2 model: “I use it quite frequently to message people, check information and manage my schedule. I try to limit distractions when I need to concentrate on an assignment.”
Q3 model: “Definitely. I can find tutorials, share files and work with classmates online, so some tasks are much easier than they were before.”
Q4 model: “I would find it difficult to live without my phone because I use it for communication, maps and everyday information. Still, I could manage without it for a short break.”
F9. Transport
Q1 model: “I usually travel by motorbike or bus, depending on where I need to go. For short journeys, I sometimes walk if the weather is comfortable.”
Q2 model: “I prefer whichever option is more practical for the journey. A motorbike is flexible, but public transport can be less stressful when traffic is heavy.”
Q3 model: “It depends on the route. Some journeys are convenient, but waiting times and crowded vehicles can make public transport less appealing.”
Q4 model: “I think more reliable services and clearer information about routes would help. If buses arrived on time and covered more residential areas, more people might use them.”
F10. Weather and seasons
Q1 model: “I prefer warm weather with a light breeze. It is comfortable enough to go outside without feeling too cold or too hot.”
Q2 model: “Yes, to some extent. Sunny weather usually makes me feel more energetic, while several days of heavy rain can make it harder to go out.”
Q3 model: “When it rains, I tend to stay indoors, study or watch something. If I have to go out, I check the forecast and bring a raincoat.”
Q4 model: “My hometown is generally warm and humid for much of the year. Places with cooler weather feel quite different, especially in the evenings.”
F11. Shopping
Q1 model: “I do, but mostly when I need something. I’m not the kind of person who goes shopping just to pass the time.”
Q2 model: “I prefer shopping online for everyday items because it is convenient to compare prices. For clothes or electronics, though, I sometimes prefer seeing the product in person.”
Q3 model: “I usually buy food, stationery and things I need for studying. Occasionally, I buy clothes or accessories, but I try not to make unnecessary purchases.”
Q4 model: “My habits have become more planned. When I was younger, I often bought things on impulse, but now I usually compare options and think about whether I really need them.”
F12. Reading and music
Q1 model: “I enjoy reading when I find a topic that interests me. I often read online articles or practical guides rather than long novels.”
Q2 model: “I listen to a mix of pop and instrumental music. It depends on my mood, and I sometimes choose instrumental music when I need to concentrate.”
Q3 model: “I usually listen to music while travelling or doing simple tasks. I avoid it when I need to focus closely on something complicated.”
Q4 model: “Yes, I enjoyed music as a child, although I did not think much about the kinds of music I liked. I read less than I do now because schoolwork takes up more of my time.”

theory.text: A study routine you can repeat

Session 1: Read one theory section and speak the worked examples aloud. Session 2: complete two or three small exercises. Session 3: plan two cue cards using keywords only. Session 4: record one full long turn, review it and repeat the weakest section.

Practise the IELTS Speaking Part 2 pattern: one minute to prepare, followed by a long turn of one to two minutes. These are task conditions, not a requirement to speak at exactly the same speed or use every second.
Important: model talks are examples, not scripts to memorise. Replace people, places, events and opinions with details that match your own experience.
Part 1 – Theory
1. Understand the task

In IELTS Speaking Part 2, the examiner gives you a task card (often called a cue card). It asks you to talk about a person, place, object, experience, activity or idea. You normally have one minute to make notes and then speak for one to two minutes. The examiner may ask a brief question after your talk before moving to Part 3.

rows: What it means for your talk
Focus on the central topic rather than trying to cover every possible angle.
Use them as a checklist for relevant content, not as four separate mini-answers.
Write keywords, names, times, places and useful phrases—not complete sentences.
Develop a connected talk with a beginning, middle and ending.
Develop the topic sufficiently; do not add irrelevant details just to fill time.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE • Cue card: Describe a useful skill you learned. You should say what it is, when and how you learned it, who helped you, and explain why it is useful. Notes: basic cooking / last summer / watched family member, practised weekends / independence, saves money.
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES • The cue card supplies the topic and directions. Select connected details and develop them into a coherent talk.
2. Read the cue card strategically
Identify the main topic noun phrase, notice the instruction verb (describe, talk about, explain), then scan the bullet points and decide what information each one asks for.

rows: Who they are, how you know them, qualities, a specific example, why they matter.
Listing adjectives without showing them through an example.
Location, appearance, atmosphere, what you do there, why it matters.
Giving only an address or general opinion.
When and where, people involved, sequence, outcome, feelings and significance.
Jumping between events without a clear timeline.
What it is, how you got it, appearance/use, personal value.
Describing appearance but ignoring its importance.
What it involves, how you started, frequency, benefits or challenges.
Explaining the activity generally but not your own experience.
Situation, options, choice, reasons, result and reflection.
Saying only what you chose without explaining why.

theory.text: 3. Use a flexible structure: Opening → Development → Reflection
This is a planning aid, not a rigid formula. Adapt it to the topic.

rows: Name the topic and establish context.
I’d like to talk about… / The first thing that comes to mind is…
Add details, an example, a sequence or a contrast.
What I remember most is… / At first… but later…
Explain why it mattered, how you felt or what changed.
Looking back… / What made it memorable was… / Since then…

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE • “I’d like to talk about a day trip I took with two friends last year. We left early, visited a coastal town and tried a local dish. The weather changed in the afternoon, so we spent some time in a small café. It was memorable because we had time to talk without worrying about university deadlines.”
HOW THE THEORY APPLIES • The talk has a clear starting point, connected details and a reflection. It does not need a dramatic story to be interesting.
4. Make useful notes in one minute
Use notes as memory triggers. Divide the page into context, main details, example or sequence, and meaning or feelings.

rows: Minh / classmate / helped coding project / stayed after class / patient
Specific cues trigger a concrete example.
last summer → first attempt → difficult → practised weekly → improved
Keywords are quicker to write and easier to speak from.
A focused talk is easier to follow.

theory.text: Write nouns, verbs, dates and adjectives—not every connecting word.
Choose details you can explain comfortably; an ordinary experience is fine.
Make sure the notes cover the cue-card prompts.
Leave a few seconds to check the order and final point.
5. Develop ideas instead of listing them
Turn each keyword into a small unit: make a point, explain it, and add an example or consequence. For stories, use sequence; for people and places, group related details.

rows: “She is patient. When I struggled with a presentation, she helped me practise twice.”
Makes an event easy to follow.
At first… / A little later… / By the end…
Explains why something happened or mattered.
Because I practised regularly, I became more confident.
I used to avoid speaking, but now I volunteer more often.
The experience taught me to ask for help earlier.

theory.text: 6. Keep the talk coherent

rows: I’d like to talk about… / The example I have in mind is…
Another thing I remember is… / What stands out is…
Do not repeat the same point.
Use when there is a real timeline.
The main reason was… / This was partly because…
Looking back… / That’s why… / Since then…
Avoid a conclusion that repeats everything.

theory.text: 7. Use topic vocabulary naturally
A few precise collocations are usually more helpful than several rare words. Choose language you can pronounce and use accurately.

rows: reliable, easy to get along with, give practical advice, set a good example
“He gives practical advice without making me feel embarrassed.”
peaceful atmosphere, within walking distance, get away from the crowds
“It has a peaceful atmosphere, especially early in the morning.”
step out of my comfort zone, a sense of achievement, things did not go to plan
“Finishing the project gave me a sense of achievement.”
come in handy, sentimental value, rely on, practical purpose
“It comes in handy when I need to take notes.”
pick up a skill, make steady progress, learn through trial and error
“I learned through trial and error rather than a formal course.”
look forward to, get together, go smoothly, a change of pace
“The celebration was a welcome change of pace after exams.”

theory.text: 8. Grammar choices for a long turn

rows: “We were walking back when it started to rain.”
“I used to be nervous about speaking in public.”
“I’d like to visit again if I get the chance.”
Relative clauses: who / which / that / where
“It’s a café where I often study.”

theory.text: Do not force every tense into one answer. Choose grammar that matches the time and meaning.
9. Fluency, pronunciation and recovery
Speak at a manageable pace; fluency is not speaking as fast as possible.
Group words into meaningful chunks rather than pausing after every word.
If you forget a detail, move on to another relevant point instead of restarting.
If you do not know a word, explain it in simpler language.
Record yourself and listen for long silences, repeated ideas and unclear word endings.
WORKED EXAMPLE • If you forget a place name: “I can’t remember the name of the café, but it was a small place near the river, and it had a lovely view.”
10. Common mistakes to avoid

rows: Uses the minute for writing rather than planning.
Write keywords and a clear sequence.
The talk sounds like a list.
Use an opening and connect details.
Hard to remember and deliver naturally.
Use a plausible experience and develop it.
Give an example, result or reflection.
Explain one detail or why it mattered.
Aim for a sufficiently developed talk.

theory.text: 11. Assessment criteria in practical terms

rows: Maintain a natural pace, organise the talk and link ideas clearly.
Use relevant vocabulary and collocations; paraphrase when a word is missing.
Use accurate sentences and a suitable range of structures and tenses.
Make words intelligible; use clear stress, chunking and a manageable pace.

theory.text: These are study explanations, not a band-score calculator. A single practice talk cannot reliably determine an overall Speaking band.
12. A 10-second checklist
Have I identified the central topic?
Do my notes cover the cue-card prompts?
Is there a clear order?
Do I have specific details or an example?
Can I explain why it matters or how I felt?
Are my notes keywords rather than a script?

guide.text: Part 3 – Planning guide
The aim is to prepare a route for your talk, not to write a memorised speech. Give yourself one minute and write keywords only. Then look away from the notes and speak.
A reusable one-minute planning worksheet

rows: When? Where? Who was involved? How did it begin?
What are two details or actions worth describing?
What specific moment, challenge or example can I explain?
Why does it matter? How did I feel? What changed?
Do the notes cover the prompts and follow a clear order?

guide.text: Worked planning example
Cue card: Describe a skill you would like to learn.
Possible opening • “A skill I’d really like to develop is photography, particularly taking better pictures when I travel.”
How to use the plan • The notes suggest motivation, a learning method, a challenge and personal value. They are not complete sentences.
Planning worksheets P1–P10
P1. A person who influenced you
Plan with keywords: Who they are / how you know them / specific thing they did / influence.
P2. A place you enjoy visiting
Plan with keywords: Location / atmosphere / what you do / memorable detail / why you return.
P3. A useful object
Plan with keywords: What it is / how you got it / how you use it / example / why it matters.
P4. A memorable day
Plan with keywords: When and where / people / sequence / best moment / feelings.
P5. A skill you learned
Plan with keywords: Skill / when and why / how you learned / challenge / result.
P6. A time you helped someone
Plan with keywords: Who / situation / what you did / response / feelings.
P7. A celebration
Plan with keywords: What was celebrated / where and with whom / activities / atmosphere / significance.
P8. A film or book
Plan with keywords: Title/type / when experienced / main idea / favourite part / recommendation.
P9. A journey
Plan with keywords: Destination / reason / travel method / event or view / impression.
P10. A goal you achieved
Plan with keywords: Goal / reason / steps / obstacle / result and lesson.
How to review a plan
Can I identify the topic in the first sentence?
Do the notes cover each cue-card prompt?
Is there a logical sequence or grouping?
Do I have a specific example, not just adjectives?
Does the final point explain significance, feelings or a lesson?
Can I speak without reading complete sentences?

small.text: Part 2 – Small exercises
Complete these tasks before checking the suggested answers. Say responses aloud when the task involves speaking. Times are practice estimates.
E1. Identify the cue-card focus
Allow 5 minutes. Identify the main topic and the information the talk should cover.
Describe a person who has influenced you. Say who the person is, how you know them, what they have done, and how they influenced you.

E2. Turn vague notes into useful notes
Allow 6 minutes. Improve each weak note set by adding an action, place, time, person or result.
E3. Put a story in order
Allow 4 minutes. Arrange the notes into a logical order, then tell the story in 5–7 sentences.

A. finally finished the presentation and felt relieved • B. realised the slides were incomplete the night before • C. practised the opening with a classmate • D. gave a university presentation last semester • E. divided the remaining work and corrected the slides
E4. Develop a keyword
Allow 8 minutes. Choose three topics. Speak two or three sentences for each: point → explanation → example or result.
patient teacher

E5. Add reflection
Allow 6 minutes. Add a sentence explaining why each experience mattered. Avoid simply repeating “It was good.”
I learned to cook a simple meal on my own. → Reflection: __________________________________________

rows: A. Description → use → why it matters

small.text: E7. Replace repetition with detail

“The trip was exciting. It was exciting from beginning to end.”

“I borrowed a tripod to keep my camera steady.”
“We went to a waterfall during our holiday.”
“She gave me a handwritten note before I left.”
“I felt overwhelmed when I had several deadlines.”

Describe a time you helped someone. Say who you helped, what the situation was, what you did, and how you felt about helping them.

Identify the main weakness: no clear structure, too vague, repetitive, tense mismatch, overcomplicated language, or insufficient reflection. Suggest one improvement.
“I want to talk about a person. He is good. He is very good. I like him.”
“Last year I go to a competition and I was nervous.”
“First, there was a thing, and then something happened, and it was amazing.”
“This extraordinary individual constitutes an indispensable component of my personal development.”

review.text: Part 5 – Complete answer key

These are suggestions, not the only correct responses. Personalise the details and use your own truthful experiences. The model talks demonstrate organisation and development, not official examiner responses.
Answers for E1
Person/influence: identify the person, relationship, action or quality, and its effect on you.
Useful object: identify it, how you obtained it, its practical use, and why it helps.
New experience: name the activity, establish when/where and who was there, describe what happened, and explain your feelings.
Place: identify the location, describe its atmosphere, explain what you do there, and give a personal reason.
Suggested approaches for E2–E8

rows: Friend: classmate / explained a difficult topic / before exam / helped me prepare. Park: near home / shaded path / walk after class / quiet in evening. Phone: bought last year / timetable and messages / daily use / keeps tasks organised. Trip: coastal town / last summer / bus with friends / unexpected rain / café stop.
D → B → E → C → A. Start with context, introduce the problem, explain the response, mention preparation and finish with the outcome.

Patient teacher: explain a difficult idea with an example. Crowded market: describe sounds and what you bought. Old photograph: say who is in it and what memory it brings back. Learning to cycle: describe first attempt, difficulty and progress. Team project: explain your role and result.
Example: “It mattered because I realised I could manage a basic task independently.” Explain a lesson, change, relationship or personal meaning.
Memorable event → B. Person you admire → C. Useful object → A. Skill learned → D.

Place: “It had a quiet garden and a view of the river, so I stayed there to read.” Cousin: “He checked my slides and practised questions with me.” Trip: “We missed the bus, found another route and arrived just before sunset.”

Tripod: a three-legged stand that holds a camera still. Waterfall: a place where water flows over a high edge of rock. Handwritten: written by hand rather than typed. Overwhelmed: feeling as if everything is too much to deal with at once.

“Last year I went to a competition and felt nervous.”
No clear structure and vague detail
Describe a specific event in chronological order.
Use natural words and a concrete example.
