Full practice: model answers
F1. Education and learning

Q1. Schools should teach practical skills because academic knowledge alone does not prepare students for every everyday decision. For example, basic financial planning can help young adults manage a budget and avoid unnecessary debt. These skills can be taught alongside academic subjects rather than replacing them.

Q2. I think both can be effective for different reasons. Teachers can respond to questions and notice confusion, while digital resources let students review material at their own pace. A combination is often useful, provided students receive guidance about which resources are reliable.

Q3. Access has become more flexible in many places. Students can use online lessons, digital libraries and recorded lectures, whereas access in the past often depended more heavily on local schools and printed resources. However, internet access and educational quality still vary.

Q4. Yes, because knowledge and working practices continue to change. Adults may need to learn new digital tools or develop communication skills as their jobs change. Continuing education can also be personally rewarding, although people need time and affordable opportunities to take part.
F2. Technology and communication

Q1. Messaging is quick and convenient, and people can reply when they have time rather than arranging a call. It is also useful for sharing links, photos or practical details. However, a phone call may be better when a conversation is emotional or complicated.

Q2. I think it has done both. It helps friends and relatives stay in touch across long distances, especially through video calls. On the other hand, online interaction can become superficial if people are distracted or rarely meet in person, so the effect depends on how technology is used.

Q3. They may do so, partly because of different experience and needs. Younger people often use digital services for study, entertainment and social networking, while some older users may prioritise messaging family or accessing practical services. These are only general tendencies, not rules for every person.

Q4. Communication may become more immediate and personalised as tools improve. For example, translation features could make it easier for people who speak different languages to communicate. Still, privacy, misinformation and unequal access are likely to remain important concerns.
F3. Work and careers

Q1. People often consider salary, stability, personal interests and opportunities to develop. The importance of each factor varies with a person's situation; for example, someone supporting a family may prioritise reliable income, while a recent graduate may value learning opportunities.

Q2. I would not say one is always more important. A fair salary is essential for financial security, but a high income may not compensate for unsafe conditions or constant stress. Ideally, people find a balance between reasonable pay, meaningful work and a manageable schedule.

Q3. Technology has changed how many people communicate and complete tasks. Some can work remotely or collaborate with colleagues in other countries, while routine tasks may be automated. However, not every job can be done online, and some workers face new pressure to learn unfamiliar tools.

Q4. Employers should provide a safe workplace, fair treatment and clear expectations. They can also support training and reasonable work-life boundaries. These responsibilities can benefit workers and the organisation, because people are more likely to perform well when they feel respected.
F4. Environment and communities

Q1. People may find change difficult when the convenient option is also the harmful one. For example, someone may use a car because public transport is unreliable, even if they want to reduce emissions. Habits, cost and access all affect whether people can change their behaviour.

Q2. Governments can make recycling easier by providing clear instructions, accessible collection points and consistent waste services. They can also encourage businesses to reduce unnecessary packaging. Information is useful, but people are more likely to recycle when the system is convenient.

Q3. Both have responsibilities. Individuals can reduce waste and make thoughtful choices, but organisations and governments control many larger systems, such as public transport, energy and product packaging. Cooperation is more realistic than expecting one group to solve everything.

Q4. People may adopt more sustainable habits if low-waste products and public transport become easier to use. However, progress will depend on infrastructure, affordability and policy, not just personal motivation. I would expect gradual change rather than a complete transformation everywhere.
F5. Cities and the countryside

Q1. Large cities often offer a wider range of jobs, universities, hospitals and public services. People may move there to study or improve their career prospects. However, high housing costs can make city life difficult, so the benefits depend on someone's priorities and income.

Q2. The main disadvantages are often congestion, expensive housing and noise. These can increase stress and make daily journeys longer. Some people also feel less connected to their neighbours, although this varies a great deal between neighbourhoods.

Q3. Cities can support families by providing safe parks, affordable childcare, reliable public transport and accessible healthcare. These services make daily life easier, especially for parents who work. Good housing and safe streets are equally important.

Q4. Some people may move to smaller towns if remote work remains practical and local services improve. They could enjoy more space and lower costs. Still, people who need specialised jobs or universities may continue to prefer large cities.
F6. Family and relationships

Q1. Spending time together helps family members share experiences and understand one another's concerns. It does not necessarily require expensive activities; eating together or taking a walk can create opportunities to talk. The important thing is giving each other attention.

Q2. Family roles have become more varied in many societies. More women work outside the home, and some families share childcare and household tasks more equally. However, changes differ by culture, income and individual circumstances, so there is no single pattern.

Q3. Yes, it can help children understand different perspectives and learn patience. Older relatives may share experiences, while children can introduce them to new interests or technology. These relationships work best when people treat one another respectfully and have opportunities to interact.

Q4. Digital tools make regular contact easier through messages and video calls. People can also plan visits and share important events online. Nevertheless, online contact may not replace physical presence entirely, so making time for visits can still matter.
F7. Health and lifestyle

Q1. Busy schedules, tiredness, cost and limited access to facilities can make healthy habits difficult. People may know that exercise is beneficial but struggle to fit it around work or study. Small, realistic routines are often easier to maintain than sudden, demanding changes.

Q2. Schools have an important role because children spend much of their time there and can learn basic information about sleep, food and exercise. Families also influence daily habits, so cooperation between school and home is likely to be more effective than relying on teachers alone.

Q3. Modern life can save time through technology, but it can also blur the boundary between work and rest. Notifications and long screen hours may make it harder to relax. The effect depends on a person's job, responsibilities and how they manage their time.

Q4. Communities can provide safe walking paths, parks, sports groups and low-cost activities. These options make exercise more accessible to people with different incomes and abilities. Campaigns can raise interest, but convenient facilities are likely to make participation easier.
F8. Culture and traditions

Q1. Traditions can connect people with their history and create a shared sense of belonging. Festivals, food and ceremonies may bring families and communities together. Their importance varies, and not everyone will relate to every tradition in the same way.

Q2. Yes, because local history can help young people understand how their communities developed and why places have particular meanings. It can also encourage respect for different experiences. Teaching it should leave room for discussion rather than presenting history as a single simple story.

Q3. Yes. A tradition can keep its central meaning while adapting its form to current needs. For example, a family celebration may use modern technology to include relatives who live abroad. Some practices may also need to change if they cause harm or exclude people.

Q4. Globalisation may introduce new music, food and ideas, which can enrich local culture. At the same time, widely marketed products can overshadow smaller traditions. Local communities can preserve what matters to them while still being open to outside influences.
F9. Shopping and consumer behaviour

Q1. Some purchases are driven by emotion, advertising or social pressure rather than real need. Buying something new can briefly improve a person's mood, and online shopping makes it easy to act on an impulse. Planning a budget and waiting before buying can help people make more considered choices.

Q2. Advertising can make products appear attractive by linking them with status, happiness or success. Repeated exposure may also make a product feel familiar. However, people do not respond to all advertising in the same way, and price, quality and personal needs still influence decisions.

Q3. Yes. Local shops can offer personal service, provide convenient access and contribute to neighbourhood life. Online shopping may offer a wider selection and easy price comparisons, so each has advantages. Many customers choose based on the product and the service they need.

Q4. People can make a shopping list, compare quality rather than only price, and pause before buying non-essential items. They can also check whether an item will be used regularly. These habits do not eliminate all impulse purchases, but they can make spending more intentional.
F10. Media and information

Q1. People follow distant events because they may affect the economy, safety, travel or issues they care about. News can also help them understand other societies. However, constant exposure to distressing stories can be overwhelming, so people may need to choose reliable sources and take breaks.

Q2. They can check who published the information, compare it with other reputable sources and look for evidence rather than relying on a headline. It is also useful to distinguish a factual report from opinion. If a claim seems surprising, checking it before sharing can prevent misinformation from spreading.

Q3. Social media allows more people to share opinions quickly and participate in public discussions. It can help important issues reach a wider audience, but it can also spread rumours or encourage hostile exchanges. The quality of discussion depends on platform design and how users behave.

Q4. Yes, because students encounter a large amount of online content. They should learn to check sources, recognise persuasive language and compare claims. These skills can help them make informed decisions beyond school, not just complete assignments.
F11. Travel and tourism

Q1. Travel gives people a chance to experience different landscapes, food and ways of life. It can also provide a break from daily routines. Some people travel for education or work rather than leisure, so motivations vary.

Q2. Tourism can create jobs and bring income to hotels, restaurants and local guides. Visitors may also support cultural sites and small businesses. The benefits are greater when local residents receive a fair share of the income and tourism is managed responsibly.

Q3. Large numbers of visitors can create congestion, litter and pressure on housing or natural areas. Popular sites may become crowded, making daily life more difficult for residents. Planning visitor numbers and investing in local infrastructure can reduce some of these problems.

Q4. Travel may become easier to plan through digital tools, and some people may choose lower-impact transport where it is practical. Costs, climate concerns and work patterns could also influence choices. The future is likely to differ between short domestic trips and long-distance travel.
F12. Artificial intelligence and the future

Q1. AI can help people complete tasks faster, organise information and automate repetitive work. Businesses may use it to improve services, while individuals may use it for translation or planning. Its usefulness depends on accuracy, privacy and whether people understand its limitations.

Q2. Tasks involving safety, empathy, ethical responsibility or complex judgement may still need strong human oversight. For example, a tool can help organise medical information, but decisions about an individual require professional judgement and context. AI can support people without taking full responsibility away from them.

Q3. Schools can teach students how to learn independently, evaluate information and use digital tools responsibly. Communication, problem-solving and adaptability will also matter because specific job tasks may change. Students need a foundation that helps them continue learning throughout their careers.

Q4. AI may replace some tasks while creating demand for other roles, but the outcome is uncertain and will vary across industries. Some workers may need retraining as jobs change. The important question is not only how many jobs appear, but whether people can access the new opportunities.
Self-assessment checklist
☐ I answer the exact question in the opening sentence.
☐ I explain how or why instead of only listing claims.
☐ I support abstract ideas with a short example or consequence.
☐ I compare fairly and avoid absolute generalisations.
☐ I use a range of linking expressions without forcing them.
☐ I use grammar I can control and make key words clear.
☐ I can recover from a pause and return to the main point.
Practice review log
Reference note

This is an independent practice guide, not an official IELTS publication. The task description and assessment terminology follow the general IELTS Speaking format. The exercises, planning frameworks and model answers are original learning materials created for practice; they are not official band-score exemplars and do not guarantee a particular score.

theory.text: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1
A step-by-step self-study guide
Learn the theory • Practise short skills • Plan the information • Write a complete report

This guide covers charts, tables, maps and processes for IELTS Academic. Task 1 is a report describing visual information. Work through the stages in order, then return to the skills that need more practice.
Your learning route

rows: Learn what to select, how to organise it and which language to use.
Complete E1–E7 before checking your answers.
Plan W1–W11 without writing full reports.
Plan, write and revise Tasks 1–27 using the original visuals.
Compare your work with the explanations, plans and model reports.
All answers are at the end.

theory.text: A study routine you can repeat

Session 1: Read one theory section and complete a related short exercise. Session 2: Plan two visuals using the worksheet. Session 3: Write one complete report. Session 4: Check it, record your errors and rewrite the weakest paragraph. Begin untimed; later use the 20-minute routine in Part 4.

Keep longer responses in a notebook or separate document. The response lines are for brief notes. Suggested answers are examples of valid approaches, not scripts to memorise or examiner-awarded band scores.
Markdown navigation: Theory | Small exercises | Planning | Full writing | Answer key.
Part 1 Theory
Know the task and the report structure
Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. Use full sentences and connected paragraphs in a neutral or academic style. Task 2 contributes twice as much as Task 1 to the Writing score. [1]

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Suppose a chart shows the proportion of commuters using buses and bicycles in two cities in 2010 and 2020. A suitable report would introduce those two modes and places, summarise the strongest overall contrast, and then give selected numbers.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The job is to REPORT the information, not argue that cycling is healthier. First name the subject, place and period; next choose the two biggest patterns for the overview; finally support them with the chart values. This shows how a selective 150-word report differs from an opinion essay.
Your job: select, summarise and compare

Report what the visual shows. Include the main features and enough detail to support them. Do not add personal opinions, background knowledge or reasons that the visual does not establish. A higher birth rate and a younger population may appear together; the table alone does not prove one caused the other.

rows: Visual type, topic, place, time and units where relevant. Paraphrase accurately.
Two or three main trends, contrasts, changes or process features.
Selected figures, comparisons, locations or stages.
The remaining main features, with supporting detail.

theory.text: Four paragraphs are a useful starting point, not a compulsory rule. The overview can follow the introduction or come at the end. A separate opinion or argumentative conclusion is unnecessary.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Illustrative chart: in City A, cycling increases from 10% to 30%, while bus use falls from 50% to 35%. In City B, cycling stays near 15%. Overview: “Cycling became substantially more common in City A, while City B showed little change.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The example selects the standout development and the contrast rather than listing every percentage. “Became more common” is a description of the shown data; “because the council built new paths” would be an invented cause unless it appears in the visual.
Introduction versus overview
Introduction: “The chart compares the proportions of male and female teachers in six types of UK educational institution in 2010.” This identifies the task.
Overview: “Women formed the large majority in nursery and primary education, whereas men predominated at university level. College teaching staff were evenly divided.” This selects the main features.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Question: a bar chart compares renewable electricity shares in four countries in 2015 and 2025. Introduction: “The bar chart compares the proportion of electricity generated from renewable sources in four countries in 2015 and 2025.” Overview: “All four shares increased, with Country A remaining the highest in both years.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The introduction tells a reader WHAT the graphic displays: type, measure, groups and dates. The overview states the main PATTERNS and ranking. Notice that it does not require exact percentages; save the supporting values for the body paragraphs.
What the four assessment criteria mean

Task Achievement: accurate coverage, clear overview and relevant support. Coherence and Cohesion: logical grouping and clear connections. Lexical Resource: precise vocabulary. Grammatical Range and Accuracy: varied, controlled sentences. [1, 2]
Vietnamese reminder: tổng quan = bức tranh lớn; chi tiết = số liệu hoặc đặc điểm minh họa. Do not turn the overview into a list of every value.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Draft: “Bikes improved a lot. City A 10, 30. Buses were worse.” Revised: “In City A, the share of bicycle commuters rose from 10% to 30%, while bus use fell from 50% to 35%.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Task Achievement improves because both trends and values are clear; Coherence improves through the “while” contrast; Lexical Resource improves through “share” and “rose”; Grammar improves through complete, controlled clauses. A polished sentence still needs an overall overview elsewhere in the report.
Describe change accurately

rows: There was a rise in sales from 20 to 30.
There was a fall in sales to 15.
There was a recovery in sales.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Illustrative line graph: online purchases account for 10%, 12%, 25% and 27% in successive years. Description: “The proportion rose slightly at first, then increased sharply before levelling off.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Match the adjective or adverb to EACH interval: 10→12 is small, 12→25 is large, and 25→27 is small again. “Rose steadily” would conceal the faster middle stage. Do not use “fluctuated” unless values actually move up and down.
Combine the direction with the size or speed

Verb + adverb: rose gradually; fell sharply. Adjective + noun: a gradual rise; a sharp fall. “Steady” describes a consistent pattern; “stable” describes little change. A series that falls once has not necessarily fluctuated.

Use strong words such as “soared” or “plummeted” only for clearly large, rapid changes. Prefer “rose” or “fell” when the pattern is ordinary. A fall from 7,000 to 5,000 is roughly 29%, so calling it “slight” may be misleading.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Values: monthly visitors rise from 2,000 in January to 2,150 in February and 5,800 in March. “Visitor numbers increased marginally in February, before rising sharply in March.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Increased” and “rising” identify direction; “marginally” and “sharply” describe magnitude. If the time intervals are equal, speed may also be inferred, but do not claim that a small increase was “dramatic”. The word choice should be calibrated to the scale.
Keep prepositions clear

From 23% to 46% = the starting and ending values. To 46% = the ending value. By 23 percentage points = the difference between the percentages. Between 1990 and 2000 = the time span; do not write “between 1990 to 2000”.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A city’s cycling share was 18% in 2012 and 33% in 2022. Correct: “It rose FROM 18% TO 33%, an increase OF 15 percentage points, BETWEEN 2012 AND 2022.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  FROM introduces the starting level; TO introduces the ending level; OF introduces the size of the rise; BETWEEN … AND … sets the time span. The share did not rise “to 15%”, and “by 15%” would wrongly suggest a relative percentage increase.
Percentage points are different from percentage change

A share rising from 23% to 46% increases by 23 percentage points. The relative increase is 100% because (46 − 23) ÷ 23 × 100 = 100. The share doubles. “It increased by 23%” would describe a different calculation.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Example data: a pass rate increases from 40% to 50%. Percentage-point rise = 50 − 40 = 10 points. Relative percentage rise = (50 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The two answers are not interchangeable: “rose by 10 percentage points” discusses the gap between shares, while “rose by 25%” discusses the size of that gap relative to the original 40%. If unsure, report “rose from 40% to 50%” instead.
Combine two stages of a trend

“The number of factories rose to 120,000 in 2010 before falling to 10,000 in 2015.” Or: “After reaching 120,000 in 2010, the number of factories fell to 10,000 five years later.” Keep the subject clear after an introductory phrase.
Avoid unnatural phrases such as “recorded with 23%” or “the quantity witnessed a wild oscillation”. Clear alternatives are “The figure stood at 23%” and “The number fluctuated considerably”.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Values: app users total 15,000 in 2018, 45,000 in 2021 and 30,000 in 2023. “User numbers tripled between 2018 and 2021, before declining to 30,000 in 2023.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The sentence compresses two genuine stages into one readable comparison: expansion followed by contraction. “Tripled” is justified because 45,000 equals three times 15,000. The final 30,000 is lower than the peak but still above the initial figure.
Compare quantities without changing the meaning

rows: the number of people / cars / factories
the percentage of time spent online
the number of users, if only time shares are shown
The figure for Australia was higher than that for Spain.
fewer teachers; less water; a lower percentage
the largest share; 39% was the largest category
the majority, when the share is below 50%

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Illustrative table: 60% of adults drink tea daily, against 45% who drink coffee daily. “Tea was consumed daily by 15 percentage points more adults than coffee.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The subjects remain comparable (shares of adults). The difference is 60−45 = 15 percentage points. Do not write “15% more people” if you mean percentage points, or say tea was “twice as popular” when the ratio is only 60:45.
Four useful comparison patterns
Australia received about 41,000 British emigrants, compared with 35,000 in Spain.
About 41,000 people moved to Australia, while around 35,000 chose Spain.
The figure for Australia was about 6,000 higher than that for Spain.
Around 41,000 and 35,000 British people moved to Australia and Spain respectively.
“While” and “whereas” introduce contrasting clauses. They do not require a comparative adjective. “Compared with” is followed by a noun phrase or figure; it also does not require “higher” or “lower”.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  City X has 80 public parks and City Y has 50. (1) “City X had 80 parks, compared with 50 in City Y.” (2) “City X had 30 more parks than City Y.” (3) “While X had 80, Y had 50.” (4) “X and Y had 80 and 50 parks, respectively.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Each sentence preserves the same comparison while changing grammar. “More … than” requires an explicit comparable noun; “while” connects two complete clauses; “respectively” works only when the noun and number orders correspond.
Use ratios carefully

“Twice as many people” describes counts; “twice as much water” describes an amount. “Three times as high” is clearer than the ambiguous “three times higher”. If two values are 20 and 60, say “60 was three times the figure of 20”.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A table shows 40 buses and 80 taxis. Correct: “There were twice as many taxis as buses.” A second table shows 60 litres of water versus 20 litres: “The first system used three times as much water as the second.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Countable items use “many”; uncountable quantity uses “much”. Always compute the ratio before using “twice” or “three times”. “80 taxis were twice higher” is grammatically misleading; repeat the thing counted so readers know exactly what is doubled.
Paraphrase precisely

Visitors are people; visits are occasions. Applicants are not necessarily enrolled students. Population is not population density. Income, revenue and profit are not automatically interchangeable. Keep the chart’s meaning even if you repeat a key word.
Prefer “accounted for”, “represented”, “stood at” and “was higher than”. Avoid “domineering”, “outperformed” or “outnumbered” when simply comparing percentages or hours.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Source title: “Average number of visits to museums per resident”. Safe introduction: “The chart shows the average number of museum visits made by each resident.” Unsafe: “The chart shows how many residents visited a museum.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Visits and visitors are different units: one resident can make several visits. Preserve that distinction even when the rewritten sentence repeats “visits”. Precision is more important than replacing every phrase with a new synonym.
Read charts and choose the main features
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Imaginary bar chart: four countries have recycling rates of 70%, 68%, 30% and 28%. Overview: “The first two countries recycled a markedly larger share of waste than the other two.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Rather than listing all four figures in an overview, spot the two clear clusters. In the body, group the high-rate pair and the low-rate pair and cite their values. This turns observation into a coherent report structure.
First decide whether time changes

rows: What rose, fell or changed rank? What were the main turning points?
Rising versus falling series; or earlier versus later periods.
What was highest or lowest? Where were the biggest contrasts or similarities?
Higher group versus lower group; or related categories.
What does each whole represent? Which shares dominate?
Compare the same category across pies, then other important shares.
Which rows and columns share the same units and meaning?
Group similar measures; keep money, years and percentages distinct.
What is the main message of each visual? Can they be compared directly?
Often one details paragraph per visual. Cover both in the overview.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A bar chart showing spending on food, housing and leisure in 2022 is a static comparison. A line chart showing the same spending from 2010 to 2022 is a time series.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  For the first, compare categories and rank the shares: “Housing accounted for the largest share.” For the second, describe change and dates: “Housing spending rose over the period.” Do not invent a trend from a single snapshot.
A chart-reading checklist
Read the title, legend and all labels before looking at the values.
Identify the unit: people, thousands, millions, percentages, money, hours or volume.
Read the dates and distinguish measured figures from forecasts.
Find two or three main features, then choose supporting details.
Check whether the graphic supports exact values or only estimates.

Use “about”, “approximately”, “just over” or “just under” for values read from a scale. Exact labels in a table can be reported directly. Do not give invented precision such as 34.73% when the axis only supports about 35%.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A vertical axis says “thousands of passengers”, with a bar at 35 for 2019. The defensible statement is “about 35,000 passengers in 2019”, not “35 passengers” or “35 million”.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Read the title and unit BEFORE forming a sentence. Next check legend, dates, and whether numbers are exact labels or estimates from the scale. These checks prevent errors in Task Achievement even when the grammar sounds fluent.
Do not force a total or a causal story

Selected categories may not add up to 100%. Report the values shown; do not invent missing categories or adjust the data. Two mixed visuals may show related changes without proving a cause. Write “Spending and participation both increased”, rather than “Participation caused spending to increase”.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A survey reports 55% using streaming services and 40% using radio. It permits overlap: respondents may use both. Safe: “Streaming was more widely used than radio.” Unsupported: “Only 5% used neither platform.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The two percentages do not necessarily form parts of a single whole because categories may overlap. Similarly, if sales rise when advertising rises, report the parallel trends rather than asserting advertising caused the increase.
Choose tenses from the task

Finished dates: “rose”, “accounted for”. No date: “shows”, “accounts for”. A series ending at the chart’s “present day”: present perfect can summarise the whole period. Forecasts: “is projected to reach”. A forecast made in 1990 for 2000: “was predicted to reach”, followed by the actual past result.
Do not reinterpret a source’s “present day” as today’s calendar date or change a forecast into a measured fact just because time has passed.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  One table reports 2015 values; another column predicts 2035. “In 2015, solar power provided 12% of the total; it is projected to account for 35% in 2035.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Use past simple for completed observations and a projection verb for future estimates. The tense follows the information status in the chart, not today’s date. Avoid writing “rose to 35% in 2035” as if the projected outcome had already been measured.
Describe maps and proposed changes

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Two maps show a riverside park in 2000 and its proposed redesign. A playground will replace a car park, but the river and entrance will remain. Overview: “The proposal replaces vehicle space with recreation while retaining the main access and riverfront.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Group changed and unchanged features before describing locations. Use proposal language (“is planned to”, “will be built”) rather than factual past change, and mention north/south only if the map establishes direction.
Read the place before describing the changes

Find the compass, dates, entrances, roads, rivers and other fixed landmarks. Identify additions, removals, replacements, relocations and features that remain. Group details by area or by type of development.

rows: in the north-west; south of the river; opposite the school; beside the road
The factory was replaced by a car park.
The office was converted into a museum.
The school was moved to the north of the river.
The housing area was expanded; the woodland was reduced in size.
The railway station remained in the same position.
The airfield is to be replaced by an industrial estate.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  On a north-oriented map, the railway runs across the southern edge. A warehouse north of it is replaced by apartments, while the station to the east remains.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Anchor the description to stable landmarks: “North of the railway, the warehouse was replaced by housing, whereas the station in the east remained unchanged.” This is more accurate than describing items solely as “left” and “right” without checking orientation.
Write a meaningful overview

Weak: “There were many changes and the general layout stayed the same.” Stronger: “The former mining site was converted into a visitor attraction, with museums and recreational facilities replacing most working facilities.”

Only say the layout remained unchanged if the maps actually support that claim. Be specific about stable features, such as a river or a main road. Do not assume a beach had no previous use or that a new road will reduce congestion unless the task states it.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Illustrative before-and-after maps: a former industrial island gains hotels and footpaths, while a central dock stays. Overview: “The island was transformed into a tourist destination, although the central dock remained in place.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The overview tells readers what TYPE of transformation occurred and identifies a major exception. It does not catalogue each hut, path and bench. “The island became more modern” is too vague and subjective to count as a strong overview.
Choose a sensible body structure

For a town divided by a road: describe the west first, then the east. For an island: describe buildings and accommodation, then paths, access and swimming facilities. For a current plan and a proposal: compare each existing feature with its proposed replacement.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Map: a central road separates a western housing area from an eastern business area. Western changes: houses and a playground. Eastern changes: offices and a new car park.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Write one paragraph about the west and one about the east, referring to the road as the boundary. This stops the reader mentally jumping between locations. If the task instead shows an old map versus a proposal, you could organise by replaced feature.
Use tenses naturally

Two finished dates can both use the past simple: “In 2000 there was an open space; by 2011 it had been replaced by flats.” Past perfect helps show an earlier past event, but is not required for every sentence about the earlier map. For proposals use “will be built”, “is planned” or “is proposed”.
Vietnamese reminder: vị trí → thay đổi → đặc điểm thay thế. Check the direction before choosing “north”, “south”, “left” or “right”.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Map A (1995): a field near the river. Map B (2015): a sports centre in its place. A proposed map for 2030: an extension east of that centre. “The field was replaced by a sports centre by 2015, and an extension is planned to its east.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The first change is a completed fact, so past passive “was replaced” fits. The extension is a proposal, so “is planned” avoids presenting it as completed. A past-perfect construction is optional, not a requirement for describing earlier maps.
Describe processes, cycles and anatomy

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Simplified glass-bottle process: used bottles are collected, cleaned, melted, shaped and cooled. Overview: “The process converts collected glass into new bottles through cleaning, melting and remoulding.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  This overview identifies the input, output and core transformation. Body details can group preparation (collection and washing) and manufacture (melting to cooling). Only mention machines, temperatures or durations if the diagram shows them.
Follow arrows rather than inventing stages

Identify the input, output, main stages, branches and any repeated cycle. An overview should describe the process as a whole: its start and end, or its main transformation. Count stages only when the diagram supports a clear count.

rows: Tomatoes are sorted, crushed and boiled.
Eggs hatch; larvae grow; adults lay eggs.
How is energy or fuel transferred?
Gas fuels an engine, which drives a generator.
Some juice is packaged directly; the rest is concentrated.
Where are the parts, and what is shown?
The wings lie beneath the red elytra.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Diagram: harvested beans → drying → roasting → grinding → packaging. Appropriate line: “After drying, the beans are roasted and ground before they are packaged.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Read arrows as evidence for SEQUENCE. Do not describe grinding before roasting or add fermentation if absent. If a diagram splits into two production lines, describe the branch rather than pretending that all products follow one route.
Use the passive when the material is the focus
Active: “Workers remove the seeds.” Passive: “The seeds are removed.” Form: be + past participle. Use the present simple for a general process unless the prompt gives another time frame.

Join stages clearly: “After being sorted, the paper is transported to a mill.” The paper is both sorted and transported, so the subject matches. A relative clause can identify a place: “The paper is sent to a mill, where it is cleaned and pulped.”
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Active: “A machine washes the bottles and workers sort them by colour.” Passive: “The bottles are washed and then sorted by colour.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The report focuses on bottles, not who operates each stage. The passive follows “be + past participle” and maintains the same material as subject. Do not make every sentence passive if an active subject such as “water” or “the machine” is useful and shown.
Sequence and alternatives

Useful links: initially; next; after this; once; subsequently; finally. Avoid starting every sentence with “then”. For alternatives: “The photographs can be developed at a pharmacy or by a professional photographer. Alternatively, they can be developed at home.”
For a closed cycle, explain how the final stage leads back to the beginning when this is shown. For a production diagram, do not invent recycling loops, temperatures, machinery or timings.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Two branches after washing: bottles may go directly to filling, or they can be melted and remade. “Once the bottles have been washed, some are refilled directly, whereas others are melted and reshaped.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Once” establishes the shared first stage; “whereas” signals two alternative routes. Do not use “finally” for a branch that does not end the whole process. Likewise, describe a loop only if the final arrow actually returns to the beginning.
Plan the details in two groups

Paper recycling: collection, sorting and transport / cleaning, de-inking and paper manufacture. Ketchup: preparing and processing tomatoes / bottling, checking and distribution. Orange juice: shared opening steps and direct packaging / the concentration and reconstitution route.
Now complete E1–E7. Keep the answer key closed until you have attempted each exercise.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Diagram: milk production has six stages: feeding cows, milking, cooling, transport, pasteurisation and bottling. Body 1 covers obtaining and storing raw milk; Body 2 covers processing and packaging.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Grouping by function makes a six-stage description easier to follow and reduces repeated “then”. The overview can say that raw milk is processed into packaged milk, while the body paragraphs retain the precise order within each group.

guide.text: Part 3 Information planning
Plan information before writing
In Task 1, planning means selecting and grouping what is shown. You do not need to brainstorm opinions or invent examples. Use this worksheet for W1–W11 and for every full writing task.

rows: Dynamic / static / mixed / map / process / cycle / anatomy

guide.text: The planning task for W1–W11

For each visual, complete the six worksheet steps. Write a one-sentence introduction and a one- or two-sentence overview. List the two detail-paragraph groups and the main evidence for each. Do not write a full report yet.
Each workshop has a specific focus below. Suggested introductions, overviews, grouping and supporting evidence are all in Part 5. Other accurate groupings are possible.
Progression
W1–W4: charts and comparable tables. W5: a table with different units. W6–W8: maps. W9–W10: mixed visuals. W11: a process. Then use Part 4 to turn the same planning skills into complete reports.
Choose one workshop at a time. Move on when your overview captures the biggest features and each detail group has a clear reason for being together.

small.text: Part 2 Small exercises
E1 · Rewrite trend sentences
Aim: change the grammar while keeping the figures and meaning. Write one sentence for each item using the required opening. Answers are in Part 5, E1.
The share of electricity generated rose from 23% in 1990 to 46% in 2000. Begin: “There was …”
The number of people commuting by car fell from 7,000 in 1990 to 5,000 in 2000. Begin: “A fall …”
The number of website visitors fluctuated between 12,000 and 20,000 from 1990 to 1995. Begin: “There were …”
Household spending on shoes remained at $320 in each of the last two years. Begin: “There was no …”
The annual income of Burney’s Bakery peaked at $3 million in 1988. Use: “reached a peak of”.
The number of university applicants fell to 8,000 in 2005, then recovered to 16,000 in 2015. Begin: “After …”
The number of factories rose to 120,000 in 2010, then fell sharply to 10,000 in 2015. Use: “before”.
E1 follow-up: quantify the change
For item 1, give (a) the increase in percentage points, (b) the relative percentage increase, and (c) one verb describing the ratio between the final and initial values.
E2 · Choose precise words and comparisons
Choose the correct option. Then correct the four comparison sentences. Answers are in Part 5, E2.
The (number / amount) of teachers rose.
The (number / amount) of water used fell.
At 39%, housing was the (largest category / majority of all spending).
A chart of visits to a website directly measures (visits / individual visitors).
The share rose from 20% to 30%, an increase of (10% / 10 percentage points).
The number of applicants is necessarily the same as the number enrolled: (true / false).
Water use was (twice as much as / twice as many as) the previous level.
The table gives the population, so it directly shows population density: (true / false).
Correct these sentences
The percentage of men was 60,000.
Housing accounted for 26%, outnumbering the 21% figure for Canada.
While 40% of men watched television, whereas 30% of women did so.
The figures for Spain and Australia were 35,000 and 41,000 respective.
Explain your choice
Why is “fewer teachers” correct, but “less water” correct? Write one sentence explaining the difference.
E3 · Rank and compare destinations
Use the 2004 chart. Values read from bars are approximate. Complete the nine gaps with the word bank, using each item once. Then write two comparison sentences. Answers are in Part 5, E3.

small.alt: Hình trong tài liệu IELTS_Writing_Task_1_No_Vertical_Lines. Mở ảnh gốc để xem chi tiết.

small.text: British emigration to five destinations in 2004
Word bank: largest; followed; contrast; fewer; lower; than; respectively; twice; similar.
Australia received the ___ number of British emigrants.
It was ___ by Spain.
In ___, the figure for France was only about 23,000.
___ people moved to Spain than to Australia.
The figure for Spain was about 6,000 ___ than Australia’s.
More people chose Australia ___ Spain.
Spain and the USA received about 35,000 and 24,000 emigrants ___.
Australia’s total was less than ___ that of New Zealand.
France and New Zealand recorded ___ totals.
Write independently
A. Compare Australia and Spain using “while”. B. Compare France and New Zealand using “approximately the same”.
E4 · Separate an overview from unsupported claims
For each statement, mark it: O = useful overview; D = supporting detail; U = unsupported or inaccurate. Correct every U statement. Answers are in Part 5, E4.

Use these facts: annual primary teaching hours are about 600 in Japan, Spain and Iceland, and 900 in the USA; upper-secondary hours are about 650, 1,000, 800 and 1,100 respectively. In a separate survey, parental sports spending and children’s swimming participation both rise. A population table shows the birth rate falling while the over-65 share rises.
The USA had the highest teaching hours at both levels described.
Primary teachers in Japan taught for about 600 hours per year.
American teachers taught more because their schools were better funded.
Increased swimming participation caused parents to spend more.
The declining birth rate caused the over-65 share to rise.
Teaching hours were higher at upper-secondary than primary level in all four countries.
E4 follow-up: organise the facts
Using only the teaching-hour facts above, write a two-sentence overview and name two sensible detail-paragraph groups. Do not add reasons for the differences.
Keep this distinction clear
An overview identifies a pattern; detail illustrates it. A claim about why a pattern exists needs evidence. When the task gives only values, describe the values and comparisons.
E5 · Build passive process sentences
The diagram shows how black-and-white photographs are produced. Convert the eight notes into present-simple passive sentences. Then join sentences 2 and 3 with “After”. Answers are in Part 5, E5.

small.alt: Hình trong tài liệu IELTS_Writing_Task_1_No_Vertical_Lines. Mở ảnh gốc để xem chi tiết.

small.text: Black-and-white photographic development process
camera / capture images and record them on film
remove / film / from camera
develop and wash / film / in development tank in darkroom
remove / negatives / from tank
view / negatives / in enlarger; enlarge and edit / images
print / images / on photographic paper
develop, fix and wash / prints / in chemical bath
dry / prints / to produce finished black-and-white photographs
Alternatives task: Write two sentences explaining that photographs may be developed (a) at a pharmacy, (b) by a professional photographer, or (c) at home. Use “either … or” and “Alternatively”.

small.text: Home electricity generation using compost, methane, an engine, a generator and a battery

A. Finally, the electricity is sent to the national grid before reaching the home. B. The diagram show a method of generating electricity for domestic use. C. Mechanical energy are converted into electrical energy by a generator, and the electricity is stored in a battery. D. Overall, the system converts compost into fuel and then electricity, using a tank, gas storage, a compressor, an engine and an generator. E. The methane flows through a pipe into a storage unit, where they is collected. F. After being compressed, the gas fuel a combustion engine, which produces mechanical energy. G. The stored gas provides the fuel for the later energy conversion stage. H. First, a steel tank is filled to three-quarters of its capacity with compost and water; the compost ferment to produce methane.

small.text: Ladybird life cycle and labelled anatomy
Word bank: stages; structure; eggs; elytra; laid; remain; emerge; pupa; end; spots; behind.

Paragraph 1: The first diagram illustrates the (1) ___ in a ladybird’s life, while the second shows its body (2) . Overall, the cycle has four stages, from (3)  to adult insect. The adult has red (4) ___ marked with black spots.

Paragraph 2: Initially, eggs are (5) ___ on the underside of a leaf and (6) ___ there for two to five days. Larvae then (7) ___ and spend 21 days in this stage. The next stage is the (8) , which lasts seven days. At the (9)  of this stage, an adult appears, and the cycle continues.
Paragraph 3: The adult’s red elytra have black (10) ___ and cover its wings and abdomen. It has six legs, eyes and antennae. The pronotum is immediately (11) ___ the head.

full.text: Part 4 Full report writing
Write and review a complete report

Use Tasks 1–27 on the following pages. Each includes its original visual. Write at least 150 words, summarising the main features and making comparisons where relevant. Use full sentences and paragraphs; do not copy the planning labels into your report.
A 20-minute routine

rows: Read labels, find the main features and group the details.
A brief plan and a clear overview.
Write the introduction, overview and two detail paragraphs.
A connected report of at least 150 words.
Check values, units, tenses, comparisons and grammar.

full.text: This is a practice routine, not a required allocation. Learn the method untimed before trying to finish within 20 minutes.
Your task on every practice page
Complete the six-step planning worksheet. Write an overview and a two-part body plan.
Write a complete report without looking at the answer key.
Use the checklist below to revise it. Then compare with the suggested plan and sample report in Part 5.
Record one data-selection mistake and one language mistake, if present; rewrite the affected sentences. If a category is already accurate, record that result.
Final checklist
Does the introduction identify the topic and time correctly?
Does the overview capture the most important features of every visual?
Are the details grouped logically and supported with relevant evidence?
Are values, units, categories and directions accurate?
Have I distinguished percentages, percentage points and actual counts?
Are forecasts and proposed developments clearly identified?
Have I avoided unsupported explanations and personal opinions?
Is the response at least 150 words and written in connected paragraphs?
The answer key supplies a possible plan and a complete report for all 27 tasks. Your grouping or wording may differ if the content is accurate and well organised.

review.text: Part 5 Complete answer key
Complete answer key

Task 1 | Task 2 | Task 3 | Task 4 | Task 5 | Task 6 | Task 7 | Task 8 | Task 9 | Task 10 | Task 11 | Task 12 | Task 13 | Task 14 | Task 15 | Task 16 | Task 17 | Task 18 | Task 19 | Task 20 | Task 21 | Task 22 | Task 23 | Task 24 | Task 25 | Task 26 | Task 27

Attempt the exercises before reading this section. Sentence rewrites, introductions, overviews and paragraph groups can have more than one correct answer. Judge alternatives by accuracy, relevance and clarity.
E1 · Suggested rewrites
There was a rise in the share of electricity generated from 23% in 1990 to 46% in 2000.
A fall from 7,000 to 5,000 was recorded in the number of people commuting by car between 1990 and 2000.
There were fluctuations in the number of website visitors between 12,000 and 20,000 from 1990 to 1995.
There was no change in household spending on shoes, which remained at $320 in each of the last two years.
The annual income of Burney’s Bakery reached a peak of $3 million in 1988.
After falling to 8,000 in 2005, the number of university applicants recovered to 16,000 in 2015.
The number of factories rose to 120,000 in 2010 before falling sharply to 10,000 in 2015.
E1 follow-up: (a) 23 percentage points. (b) 100%. (c) Doubled. The final share is twice the initial share. Do not replace “applicants” with “enrolled students” or “visitors” with “visits”.
E2 · Word choices
1 number; 2 amount; 3 largest category; 4 visits; 5 10 percentage points; 6 false; 7 twice as much as; 8 false.
E2 · Corrected comparisons
The number of men was 60,000. Alternatively, if the unit is genuinely a percentage, use a percentage value supported by the source.
Housing accounted for 26%, compared with 21% in Canada. Alternatively: “The housing share was five percentage points higher than Canada’s.”
While 40% of men watched television, 30% of women did so. Alternatively: “40% of men watched television, whereas 30% of women did so.”
The figures for Spain and Australia were 35,000 and 41,000 respectively.
Explanation: “teachers” is countable, so use “fewer”; “water” is uncountable, so use “less”. Percentages are higher or lower, rather than “outnumbering” each other.
Answers · Comparisons and overviews
E3 · Gap-fill answers
1 largest; 2 followed; 3 contrast; 4 Fewer; 5 lower; 6 than; 7 respectively; 8 twice; 9 similar.
E3 · Independent sentences

A. About 41,000 British people emigrated to Australia in 2004, while approximately 35,000 chose Spain. B. France and New Zealand received approximately the same number of British emigrants, at around 23,000 each.
Other accurate versions are possible. “While” does not require a comparative adjective, and a small estimated difference should not be described as a dramatic contrast.
E4 · Classification and correction

rows: It summarises the cross-country ranking at both levels.
The chart does not show school funding. Write: “American teachers recorded higher teaching hours than the other countries.”
The charts do not prove causation. Write: “Parental spending and swimming participation both increased.”
The table does not establish a cause. Write: “The birth rate fell while the over-65 share increased.”
It identifies a consistent contrast between the two levels.

review.text: E4 · Suggested overview and grouping

Overview: “The USA recorded the highest annual teaching hours at both levels, while primary hours were identical in the other three countries. Upper-secondary teachers taught more hours than primary teachers in every country described.”

Details paragraph 1: primary hours — about 600 in Japan, Spain and Iceland, compared with 900 in the USA. Details paragraph 2: upper-secondary hours — approximately 650 in Japan, 800 in Iceland, 1,000 in Spain and 1,100 in the USA.
A country-based grouping is also possible if it produces clear comparisons and covers both levels accurately.
Answers · Passive sentences and sequence
E5 · Eight passive sentences
Images are captured by a camera and recorded on film.
The film is removed from the camera.
The film is developed and washed in a development tank in a darkroom.
The negatives are removed from the tank.
The negatives are viewed in an enlarger, where the images can be enlarged and edited.
The images are printed on photographic paper.
The prints are developed, fixed and washed in a chemical bath.
The prints are dried to produce the finished black-and-white photographs.
Joined version: “After being removed from the camera, the film is developed and washed in a development tank in a darkroom.” The film is the subject of both actions.
Alternatives: “The photographs can be developed either at a pharmacy or by a professional photographer. Alternatively, they can be developed at home.”
E6 · Order and paragraph groups

Order: B → D → H → E → G → F → C → A. Paragraph 1: B and D, introducing the system and its overall transformation. Paragraph 2: H, E and G, describing fuel production and storage. Paragraph 3: F, C and A, describing electricity generation and home use.
E6 · Corrected sentences

B. The diagram shows a method of generating electricity for domestic use. D. Overall, the system converts compost into fuel and then electricity, using a tank, gas storage, a compressor, an engine and a generator. H. First, a steel tank is filled to three-quarters of its capacity with compost and water; the compost ferments to produce methane. E. The methane flows through a pipe into a storage unit, where it is collected. G. The stored gas provides the fuel for the later energy conversion stage. F. After being compressed, the gas fuels a combustion engine, which produces mechanical energy. C. Mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy by a generator, and the electricity is stored in a battery. A. Finally, the stored electricity is supplied to the home for domestic use.
A contains a factual problem: the national grid is not shown. G is already correct and functions as a transition. The other corrections concern agreement or the article before “generator”.
Answers · Life cycle and planning workshops
E7 · Gap-fill answers
1 stages; 2 structure; 3 eggs; 4 elytra; 5 laid; 6 remain; 7 emerge; 8 pupa; 9 end; 10 spots; 11 behind.

Paragraph 1 contains the overview after its introductory sentence. Paragraph 2 describes the life cycle; paragraph 3 describes anatomy. The elytra are the protective wing cases, so they should not simply be renamed “wings”.
E7 · Completed description

The first diagram illustrates the stages in a ladybird’s life, while the second shows its body structure. Overall, the cycle has four stages, from eggs to adult insect. The adult has red elytra marked with black spots.

Initially, eggs are laid on the underside of a leaf and remain there for two to five days. Larvae then emerge and spend 21 days in this stage. The next stage is the pupa, which lasts seven days. At the end of this stage, an adult appears, and the cycle continues.
The adult’s red elytra have black spots and cover its wings and abdomen. It has six legs, eyes and antennae. The pronotum is immediately behind the head.
W1 · British emigration

Introduction: The chart compares the numbers of British people emigrating to five destinations between 2004 and 2007. Overview: Australia remained the leading destination. New Zealand declined steadily, while Spain ended lower after a small initial increase; France and the USA varied over the period.

Details 1: Australia and Spain — about 41,000 to 44,000 for Australia, with a 2006 peak near 52,000; Spain around 35,000 to 28,000. Details 2: the smaller destinations — New Zealand about 23,000 to 20,000; France peaking near 33,000 in 2005 before falling below 20,000; the USA varying around 20,000–24,000. Unit: people, with the axis in thousands. Tense: past simple.
W2 · Leisure activities

Introduction: The chart compares the percentages of men and women taking part in eight leisure activities. Overview: Computer games were the most common male activity, while shopping led among women. Going out with friends was popular with both groups, whereas reading had low figures.

Details 1: large gaps — games about 84% of men versus 3% of women; shopping about 24% versus 75%; television about 65% versus 30%. Details 2: closer figures — friends around 70% for both; cinema and gym about 40%; music about 25–28%; reading below 10%. Unit: percentages, not counts. Tense: present simple is also valid because no date is specified; keep the choice consistent.
Answers · Planning workshops
W3 · Housing preferences
Introduction: The chart compares preferences for four types of housing in Liverpool, London and Manchester in 2009.
Overview: Flats were clearly the leading choice in Liverpool, while semi-detached houses were most popular in London and Manchester. Terraced houses had the lowest share in all three cities.

Details 1: London and Manchester — semi-detached about 37% each; detached 25% versus 35%; flats 29% versus 19%; terraced 19% versus 12%. Details 2: Liverpool — flats about 58%; semi-detached 18%; detached 15%; terraced 9%. Percentages; past simple. Do not force the city totals to add to 100%.
W4 · Consumer spending
Introduction: The table compares the proportions of consumer spending allocated to three categories in four countries in 2008.
Overview: Fast food and drinks attracted the largest share in every country, and leisure activities and education the smallest. China had the highest shares in the first two categories.

Details 1: fast food/drinks — China 28.91%, Japan 18.8%, Thailand 16.36%, Vietnam 15.77%. Details 2: shoes/watches — China 16.23%, others below 6%; leisure/education — Vietnam 3.22% and Thailand 3.2%, compared with China 2.21% and Japan 1.98%. Percentages; past simple.
Answers · Planning workshops
W5 · Australian water charges
Introduction: The table compares water charges per kilolitre and average household bills in five Australian cities.
Overview: Perth has the steepest difference between the two usage bands and the highest average bill. Melbourne has the lowest bill; Melbourne and Sydney have unchanged unit charges across the bands.

Details 1: rates — Adelaide $0.42/$1.00; Perth $0.42/$1.50; Brisbane $0.81/$0.84; Melbourne $0.78 in both bands; Sydney $0.98 in both. Details 2: bills — Perth $332, Sydney $319, Adelaide $312, Brisbane $310, Melbourne $253. Dollars per kilolitre versus dollars per household; present simple. These are usage bands, not a time trend.
W6 · Eastminster village
Introduction: The maps illustrate the transformation of Eastminster between 1999 and 2009.
Overview: The village became more developed, gaining commercial, industrial and tourist facilities. The school moved north of the river, while the river, hospital and railway station remained.

Details 1: north of the river — woodland to adventure park; houses expanded; park reduced; large house with gardens to hotel with golf course; school relocated here. Details 2: south — shopping complex on the former school site; streets of houses replaced by apartment blocks and housing; factories and warehouses on the former public-garden area; shops and hospital retained. Dates and positions; past simple, with past perfect optional where helpful.
Answers · Planning workshops
W7 · Island tourism
Introduction: The maps show an island before and after the construction of tourist facilities.
Overview: The island gained accommodation, visitor facilities and boat access, while its coastline and much of the eastern natural area were retained.

Details 1: buildings — two accommodation clusters; central reception; restaurant to its north. Details 2: movement and leisure — southern pier and vehicle track connecting the reception and restaurant; footpaths connecting accommodation and the western beach; designated swimming area. Positions rather than invented dates; past simple for the earlier state and present perfect for completed development, or a consistent before/after description.
W8 · Mine redevelopment
Introduction: The maps compare a working mine with its layout after conversion into a visitor attraction.
Overview: Industrial facilities were replaced or adapted for tourism, while the car park and underground entrance remained in their original positions.

Details 1: left and centre — office and changing room to museum; medical room to café; lorry park to souvenir shop; car park retained; mine entrance opened to visitors. Details 2: right — waste-tip areas replaced by a digger-driving track, picnic area and children’s play area, connected by footpaths. Use left/right because no compass is provided. Past simple plus present perfect is suitable for before and after.
Answers · Planning workshops
W9 · Global water use
Introduction: The graph shows worldwide water use by sector from 1900 to 2000, and the table compares Brazil and the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2000.
Overview: Water use rose in all sectors, with agriculture consistently the largest. Brazil had much higher water consumption per person than the Congo.

Details 1: graph — agriculture about 500 to 3,000 km³; industry about 100 to 1,400 km³; domestic use below 100 to about 500 km³. Details 2: table — Brazil 176 million people, 26,500 km² irrigated land, 359 m³ per person; Congo 5.2 million, 100 km², 8 m³. Keep the units distinct. Past simple. The irrigated area is 265 times as large in Brazil, but the chart does not prove it caused the per-person difference.
W10 · Family finances
Introduction: The table and pie charts compare income and spending on food and clothes for an average family in a UK city in 2010 and 2013.
Overview: Income declined while spending on food and clothes rose. Fruit and vegetables replaced meat and fish as the largest spending category.

Details 1: table — income 29,000 to 25,000; food/clothes spending 14,000 to 15,000. Details 2: pies — fruit/vegetables 26% to 30%; dairy 12% to 16%; meat/fish 29% to 23%; clothes 15% to 13%; other food 18% in both. Use the money scale as given because the reproduced table has no currency label. Past simple. A lower share does not automatically mean lower absolute spending; calculate only when useful.
Answers · Planning workshops
W11 · Paper recycling
Introduction: The flow chart shows how waste paper is recycled into usable paper.
Overview: There are six main stages, beginning with collection and ending with paper manufacture. The material is sorted and cleaned before being made into new paper.

Details 1: collection from paper banks or businesses; manual sorting by grade and rejection of unsuitable paper; transport to a mill. Details 2: cleaning and pulping, including staple removal; de-inking to remove ink and glue; production of usable paper in a paper-making machine. Present simple, mainly passive; no numerical unit or date is needed.
Model reports · Tasks 1–2
Task 1 · Three London bakeries
Suggested plan: Details 1: the overall increases at Robbie’s Bakery and Bernie’s Buns. Details 2: the decline at Lovely Loaves and the change in ranking.
The line graph compares the yearly income of three London bakeries, Bernie’s Buns, Lovely Loaves and Robbie’s Bakery, between 2000 and 2010. The figures are given in pounds.

Overall, income increased at Robbie’s Bakery and Bernie’s Buns, whereas Lovely Loaves experienced an overall decline. Lovely Loaves earned the most at the beginning, but Robbie’s became the leading bakery from 2006 onwards.

Robbie’s income remained at approximately £55,000 from 2000 to 2005. It then rose to about £60,000 in 2006 before increasing much more rapidly, reaching roughly £105,000 by 2010. Bernie’s Buns started considerably lower, at around £20,000. After some early variation, its earnings stayed close to £38,000 from 2003 to 2005, dipped slightly in 2006 and then climbed to about £65,000 at the end.

By contrast, Lovely Loaves began at just over £80,000 and peaked at approximately £93,000 in 2001. Following further fluctuations, its income fell sharply after 2004. It dropped to around £40,000 in 2008 and remained near that level for the final two years.
Task 2 · Outdoor sports
Suggested plan: Details 1: swimming and jogging/running, which end higher. Details 2: ball games and biking/roller skating, which end lower.
The line graph shows changes in the proportions of young people participating in four outdoor sports in the South West of England, from 1975 to the present day shown on the chart.

Overall, swimming and jogging or running have become more popular, while participation in ball games and biking or roller skating has declined. Swimming has overtaken ball games to become the most popular activity by the end of the period.

Swimming accounted for about 14% of young people in 1975 and 1980. Its share then rose steadily to approximately 24% in 2000 before reaching around 34% at the final point. Jogging and running began at about 7%, increased to 13% in 1985 and then fell to roughly 9% in 1995. The figure has subsequently recovered to approximately 15%.

In contrast, ball games started at around 34%, the highest initial proportion, but fell to about 20% by the end. Biking and roller skating also lost participants in percentage terms, declining from 25% to approximately 16%, despite a small recovery around 1990.
Model reports · Tasks 3–4
Task 3 · Places of Internet access
Suggested plan: Details 1: home and work. Details 2: college and library. Compare changes rather than adding the categories to a total.
The bar chart compares the percentages of people who mostly accessed the Internet at home, at work, at college or in a library in the UK in four years between 1998 and 2004.

Overall, home was the leading location in every year, despite an initial fall. Access at work became less common, while the figures for colleges and libraries fluctuated and remained well below the home figure.

In 1998, approximately 55% of people used the Internet mainly at home. This proportion fell to about 48% in 2000, recovered to 50% in 2002 and returned to roughly 55% in 2004. The workplace figure was much lower, at around 28% in both 1998 and 2000, before declining to approximately 26% in 2002 and 16% in 2004.

College access accounted for about 20% in the first two years, rose to approximately 25% in 2002 and then fell to around 18%. Library use increased from roughly 12% to 18% between 1998 and 2000, before settling at approximately 16% in the final two years.
Task 4 · Male and female teachers
Suggested plan: Details 1: nursery, primary and secondary education. Details 2: college, private training institutes and university.
The bar chart compares the proportions of male and female teaching staff in six types of educational institution in the UK in 2010.

Overall, women were much more strongly represented in nursery and primary education, whereas men formed the majority at university level. The difference between the sexes was smaller in the middle categories, with an equal distribution at colleges.

Women accounted for approximately 96% of nursery and pre-school teachers, leaving only about 4% for men. A similar pattern appeared in primary schools, where the female share was just over 90% and the male share was below 10%. At secondary level, the gap narrowed substantially: women represented roughly 55% of teachers, compared with about 45% for men.

College staff were divided equally, with each sex accounting for 50%. Men had a modest lead in private training institutes, at approximately 55%, against 45% for women. The male proportion was considerably higher at universities, reaching about 70%, while women made up the remaining 30%. Thus, the strongest male and female majorities occurred at opposite ends of the educational range.
Model reports · Tasks 5–6
Task 5 · Watching and participating in sport
Suggested plan: Details 1: football, fishing, and horse riding and racing, with large gaps. Details 2: rugby, basketball and badminton.
The bar chart compares the percentages of males who prefer watching six types of sport with the percentages who prefer participating in them in a particular country.

Overall, watching was more popular than participation in every category except fishing. Fishing had the highest participation figure, while football and horse riding and racing attracted the largest proportions of viewers.

Around 45% preferred watching football, compared with only about 10% who preferred playing it. Horse riding and racing showed a similar contrast, with approximately 45% choosing to watch and 20% choosing to participate. Fishing displayed the opposite pattern: participation reached 50%, the highest figure on the chart, whereas watching accounted for just 15%.

The gaps were smaller for the remaining sports. Basketball attracted about 37.5% as viewers and 25% as participants. For rugby, the corresponding figures were approximately 30% and 20%. Badminton also had a viewing figure of around 30%, but its participation figure was slightly higher than rugby’s, at about 25%. Consequently, badminton had the smallest difference between the two preferences.
Task 6 · Annual teaching hours
Suggested plan: Details 1: primary and secondary hours. Details 2: upper-secondary hours, comparing the four countries.
The bar chart compares the number of hours taught annually by primary, secondary and upper-secondary teachers in Japan, Spain, Iceland and the USA in 2001.

Overall, American teachers had the highest annual teaching hours at all three levels. Upper-secondary teachers taught at least as many hours as those at the other levels in every country, although the difference was particularly small in Japan.

Primary teachers in Japan, Spain and Iceland each taught for approximately 600 hours per year. The corresponding figure in the USA was considerably higher, at about 900 hours. At secondary level, Japan and Spain remained at around 600 hours, while Iceland rose to approximately 800 and the USA to just over 1,000.

Upper-secondary teaching hours varied more widely between countries. Japan recorded the lowest figure, at approximately 650 hours, only slightly above its primary and secondary totals. Iceland’s upper-secondary figure was about 800 hours, the same as its secondary figure. Spain reached roughly 1,000 hours, while the USA again had the highest total, at approximately 1,100 hours.
Model reports · Tasks 7–8
Task 7 · Household expenditure
Suggested plan: Details 1: food, housing and transportation. Details 2: health care and clothing. Note that Japan spends a slightly larger share on food than housing.
The bar chart compares the shares of expenditure allocated to five categories in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and Japan in 2009.

Overall, housing accounted for the largest share in the first three countries, while food was slightly higher than housing in Japan. Health care and clothing represented relatively small proportions in all four countries.

Housing expenditure reached 26% in the United States, compared with 24% in the United Kingdom, 22% in Japan and 21% in Canada. Food showed a different ranking: Japan had the highest share, at 23%, followed by the United Kingdom at 20%. Canada and the United States recorded lower figures of 15% and 14% respectively. Transportation was most prominent in Canada, at 20%, and least prominent in Japan, at 10%.

The remaining two categories each accounted for less than 10% everywhere. Health care represented 7% of expenditure in the United States, 4% in Canada and Japan, and only 2% in the United Kingdom. Clothing stood at 6% in Canada and the United Kingdom, compared with 4% in the other two countries.
Task 8 · Time spent on Internet activities
Suggested plan: Details 1: large contrasts in bookings, games and music/films. Details 2: social networking, research and purchases.
The pie charts compare how people aged 18–26 and 60–70 distribute their online leisure time among six activities.

Overall, social networking takes the largest share of the younger group’s time, whereas making bookings is the leading activity among older users. The greatest differences concern bookings and games, while the two groups allocate identical shares to online purchases.

People aged 60–70 spend 25% of their online time making bookings, such as travel or cinema reservations, compared with just 5% among those aged 18–26. The younger group, however, devotes 18% to playing games, against only 5% for older users. Accessing music and films also occupies a larger share among younger people, at 21%, compared with 15% in the older group.

The differences in the other categories are less pronounced. Social networking accounts for 24% of younger users’ time and 21% of older users’ time. Researching information such as health data represents 20% and 22% respectively. Finally, making purchases takes up 12% of online time in both age groups.
Model reports · Tasks 9–10
Task 9 · Water use in three areas
Suggested plan: Details 1: contrast residential and agricultural shares. Details 2: compare industrial use. California’s largest category is below 50%.
The three pie charts compare the proportions of water used for residential, industrial and agricultural purposes in San Diego County, California and the world as a whole.

Overall, residential use accounts for the largest share in San Diego and California, while agriculture dominates worldwide consumption. Industrial use is more similar across the three areas than either of the other two categories.

In San Diego County, residential consumption represents 60% of water use, considerably higher than California’s figure of 39%. The worldwide residential proportion is much smaller, at only 8%. Agriculture shows the reverse pattern. It accounts for 69% of global water consumption but just 28% in California and 17% in San Diego. Thus, the largest worldwide category is the smallest category in both American areas.

Industrial consumption stands at 23% in San Diego, which is exactly the same as the worldwide figure. California allocates a larger proportion to industry, at 33%. Its distribution is also relatively balanced: the difference between its largest and smallest categories is only 11 percentage points, compared with much wider gaps in the other two charts.
Task 10 · Sources of electricity
Suggested plan: Details 1: India and Vietnam, dominated by fossil fuels. Details 2: Sweden and Morocco, dominated by hydro power. These are country breakdowns, not a year-by-year trend.
The pie charts compare the proportions of electricity generated from fossil fuels, hydro power and nuclear power in four countries during the period 2003–2008.

Overall, fossil fuels were the main source in India and Vietnam, whereas hydro power contributed the largest share in Sweden and Morocco. Nuclear electricity was shown only in India and Sweden, with a much larger proportion in the latter.

India relied most heavily on fossil fuels, which accounted for 82% of its electricity production. Hydro power supplied 14%, while nuclear power contributed the remaining 4%. Vietnam also generated most of its electricity from fossil fuels, although the proportion was lower, at 56%. Its other 44% came from hydro power, with no nuclear contribution shown.

Sweden had a contrasting distribution. Hydro power represented 52% of production and nuclear power a further 44%, leaving only 4% for fossil fuels. Morocco was even more dependent on hydro power, which supplied 95% of its electricity. Fossil fuels accounted for the remaining 5%, and nuclear power was absent from its electricity mix.
Model reports · Tasks 11–12
Task 11 · Car production
Suggested plan: Details 1: Thailand’s consistently high output and its intermediate peak. Details 2: the opposite overall trends in Argentina and Australia.
The table compares car production in Argentina, Australia and Thailand in three years between 2003 and 2009.

Overall, Thailand produced the most cars in every year, despite a decline after 2005. Argentina’s output increased throughout the period, while Australia’s fell, allowing Argentina to overtake Australia by 2005.

Thailand manufactured 735,852 cars in 2003, substantially more than either of the other countries. Production then rose sharply to 1,162,356 in 2005 before decreasing to 999,963 in 2009. Although the final figure was below the intermediate peak, it remained well above the 2003 level and exceeded the combined output of Argentina and Australia in 2009.

Argentina began with the lowest production, at 235,088 cars, but its total increased to 352,759 in 2005 and 466,089 in 2009. This represented an almost twofold rise over the period.
